How does dataset size affect performance? Does a particular preprocessing method improve classification? These become candidates for research questions. 2. Define the research objective Convert the problem into a broad objective. For example: Objective: To evaluate the generalization performance of CNN and transformer-based models for image classification across independent datasets. Your research questions should directly support this objective. 3. Formulate the main research question A good research question should be: clear; specific; answerable; relevant to the research problem; appropriately scoped; empirically investigable. Weak How can AI improve image classification? Too broad. Better How does the choice of neural-network architecture affect image-classification performance on medical-image datasets? Even more specific How do CNN and transformer architectures differ in classification performance and computational cost when evaluated on the same medical-image dataset? The final version specifies what will be compared and what outcomes matter. 4. Identify your variables For quantitative computer science research, identify: Independent variable The factor you change or compare. Examples: model architecture; learning rate; training dataset size; data augmentation; feature-selection method. Dependent variable What you measure. Examples: accuracy; F1-score; inference latency; memory usage; training time; error rate. Control variables Factors you keep consistent. Examples: dataset; train/test split; preprocessing; hardware; evaluation metric; training budget. Example Suppose you compare CNN and transformer models. Independent variable: Model architecture ↓ Dependent variables: F1-score Accuracy Inference time ↓ Control variables: Dataset Preprocessing Train/test split Training budget This structure makes it much easier to formulate a testable hypothesis. 5. Decide whether you actually need hypotheses Not every CS study requires a hypothesis. Exploratory study You might ask: What factors influence developers' adoption of AI coding assistants? You may primarily use research questions. Experimental study You might ask: Does model A outperform model B under controlled conditions? A hypothesis is more appropriate. Design/engineering study You might ask: How can a low-latency authentication system be designed for IoT devices? The study may focus on design requirements and evaluation rather than formal hypothesis testing. So don't add hypotheses simply because a template asks for them. They should fit the research design. 6. Formulate the research question types Several types are particularly useful in computer science. A. Descriptive questions Ask what exists or what happens. What machine-learning techniques are currently used for detecting network intrusions? Useful for exploratory or literature-based studies. B. Comparative questions Compare two or more approaches. How does Random Forest compare with XGBoost for network intrusion detection? These are common in ML research. C. Relationship questions Investigate relationships between variables. What is the relationship between training-data size and model performance? D. Causal/effect questions Ask whether changing something produces an effect. Does data augmentation improve the robustness of image-classification models? These require an appropriate experimental design if you want to make causal claims. E. Design questions Ask how to construct or improve a system. How can a transformer-based model be designed to reduce inference latency while maintaining classification performance? F. Evaluation questions Ask whether a method works under particular conditions. How well does the proposed model generalize to an unseen dataset? 7. Convert research questions into hypotheses A hypothesis should make a specific, testable prediction. Suppose your RQ is: Does data augmentation improve image-classification performance? A hypothesis could be: H1: Models trained with data augmentation will achieve higher F1-scores than models trained without augmentation under the same experimental conditions. Now the variables are clear: Independent variable → augmentation vs. no augmentation Dependent variable → F1-score Controls → dataset, model, split, training procedure 8. Use null and alternative hypotheses For quantitative studies, you may formulate: Null hypothesis (H₀) There is no specified difference or effect. H₀: Data augmentation does not produce a difference in F1-score under the specified experimental conditions. Alternative hypothesis (H₁) There is a difference or effect. H₁: Data augmentation produces a difference in F1-score under the specified experimental conditions. If you have a justified directional prediction, you could formulate: H₁: Data augmentation increases F1-score. Whether a directional hypothesis is appropriate depends on your prior evidence and study design. 9. Don't make hypotheses too vague Weak H1: Transformers perform better. Better: H1: Under the same dataset, preprocessing pipeline, and training budget, the transformer model will achieve a higher F1-score than the CNN baseline. Now the hypothesis is operational and testable. 10. Be careful with "better" "Better" is meaningless unless you define better according to what. For example: Model A is better than Model B. Could mean: higher accuracy; lower error; lower latency; less memory; better calibration; better robustness; lower training cost. Instead say: Model A achieves a higher F1-score than Model B. or: Model A achieves comparable F1-score with lower inference latency. The metric should follow from the research objective. 11. Make the research questions measurable Consider: How effective is the proposed cybersecurity system? "Effective" is vague. Instead: What are the precision, recall, F1-score, and false-positive rate of the proposed intrusion-detection system on the test dataset? Now you know exactly what evidence is needed. 12. Ensure alignment between RQ, hypothesis, method, and analysis This is one of the most important principles. Think of the study as: Research problem ↓ Research objective ↓ Research question ↓ Hypothesis ↓ Variables ↓ Experimental design ↓ Data collection ↓ Statistical / computational analysis ↓ Conclusion Everything should connect. Example Problem: Current models may not generalize well across datasets. Objective: Evaluate cross-dataset generalization. RQ: How does model architecture affect cross-dataset generalization? H1: Transformer-based models will achieve higher F1-score than CNN models on the independent test dataset. Method: Train both models using the same training dataset and evaluate them on an independent dataset. Measure: F1-score, recall, precision. Now the study has a coherent structure. 13. Use multiple research questions when necessary A complex study may have one main RQ and several subquestions. Main RQ How effectively do deep-learning architectures generalize to unseen datasets? Sub-RQs RQ1: How does CNN performance compare with transformer performance on the source dataset? RQ2: How does performance change when models are evaluated on an independent dataset? RQ3: How does training-data size affect cross-dataset generalization? RQ4: What is the computational cost of each architecture? This structure prevents one enormous research question from becoming difficult to answer. 14. Example: complete ML research formulation Suppose your topic is: Deep learning for plant-disease classification Research problem Existing studies report high classification performance, but many evaluations use limited benchmark datasets. Objective To compare the performance and generalization of CNN and transformer models across plant-disease datasets. Main research question RQ1: How do CNN and transformer architectures compare in plant-disease classification performance? Additional questions RQ2: How does performance change when models are evaluated on an independent dataset? RQ3: What is the relationship between training-data size and classification performance? RQ4: How do the models differ in computational requirements? Hypotheses H1: Under a controlled experimental setup, the transformer and CNN architectures will differ in classification F1-score. H2: Model performance will decrease when evaluated on an independent dataset compared with the source test dataset. H3: Increasing the amount of training data will improve classification performance, subject to diminishing returns. Notice that H2 and H3 are predictions that can be empirically tested. 15. Qualitative research questions work differently If your computer science study involves human participants—for example, studying developers' experiences with AI coding tools—you may not need statistical hypotheses. Research question How do software developers use generative AI tools during software development? Subquestions could be: What tasks do developers delegate to AI tools? What factors influence their trust in AI-generated code? What challenges do developers experience? You could investigate these through interviews, observation, or thematic analysis. A formal hypothesis isn't necessarily required because the objective is to explore and understand experiences, rather than test a predefined numerical prediction. 16. Mixed-methods example Suppose you want to study AI coding assistants. Quantitative RQ Does use of an AI coding assistant reduce task-completion time? Quantitative hypothesis H1: Developers using the AI assistant will have lower mean task-completion times than developers in the control condition. Qualitative RQ How do developers perceive the assistant's influence on their programming workflow? You could then combine the results: The quantitative component measures whether task completion changes, while the qualitative component investigates how and why developers experience the tool differently. 17. Common mistakes Mistake 1: Asking a question that is too broad How does AI affect society? Break it into a specific population, technology, outcome, and context. Mistake 2: Making the hypothesis obvious H1: A new algorithm will improve performance. Instead specify: H1: Under the specified experimental conditions, the proposed algorithm will achieve a higher macro-F1 score than the baseline. Mistake 3: Using unsupported predictions Don't formulate: Transformers will definitely outperform CNNs. unless your literature review provides a reasonable basis for expecting that outcome. A hypothesis is a testable prediction, not a predetermined conclusion. Mistake 4: Asking multiple questions in one RQ How accurate, fast, robust, interpretable, scalable, and energy-efficient is the model? That's several research questions. Separate them. Mistake 5: Having a hypothesis that your method cannot test If your hypothesis concerns: User satisfaction but your experiment collects only: Model accuracy then the study cannot answer the hypothesis. A useful template You can formulate your study using: Research problem: Existing research shows ________, but ________ remains unclear. Research objective: This study aims to investigate ________. Main research question: How/what/to what extent does ________ affect/compare with ________ under ________ conditions? Independent variable: Dependent variable: H₀: There is no statistically detectable difference/effect in ________ under the specified conditions. H₁: ________ produces/is associated with ________ under the specified conditions. Final checklist Before finalizing your research questions and hypotheses, ask: Is the research problem clearly defined? Does each RQ address an identifiable gap? Is each RQ specific enough to investigate? Can I collect evidence to answer it? Are my variables clearly defined? Are my hypotheses testable? Do the hypotheses follow logically from the literature? Does my methodology actually allow me to answer the RQs? Are my evaluation metrics appropriate? Can I distinguish the result from my interpretation? The strongest CS studies have a visible chain from literature gap → research question → hypothesis (when appropriate) → experiment → measurement → analysis → conclusion.

prompt: Explain how to critically evaluate the validity of a paper's experimental design.
chatgpt_response: To critically evaluate the validity of a paper's experimental design, don't ask only whether the experiment was conducted correctly. Ask whether the design actually supports the claims the authors make. A useful framework is: Research question → experimental design → data → controls → measurements → analysis → conclusion If there is a weakness at any stage, the validity of the conclusion may be affected. 1. Start with the research question First identify exactly what the paper is trying to establish. For example: "Does data augmentation improve the generalization of an image-classification model?" Then ask: Does the experimental design actually test this question? If the paper compares two models but changes the dataset, preprocessing, and training procedure at the same time, it may not be able to isolate the effect of data augmentation. Check Is the research question clearly stated? Is the experiment directly relevant to it? Are the variables operationally defined? Does the experimental design allow the proposed conclusion? 2. Identify the independent and dependent variables Determine: Independent variable What is being changed? Example: Data augmentation: enabled vs. disabled. Dependent variable What is being measured? Example: F1-score. Control variables What should remain constant? Example: same dataset; same model; same train/test split; same training budget; same evaluation procedure. A valid experiment should change the factor of interest without unnecessarily changing other factors. 3. Examine the control or comparison group Ask: Compared with what? Suppose a paper proposes a new ML model and reports: Accuracy = 96%. That number has little meaning without an appropriate comparison. Look for: established baseline; previous state-of-the-art method; simple baseline; ablation model; control condition. A particularly useful question is: Is the baseline strong enough and implemented fairly? An artificially weak baseline can make a new method appear more effective than it actually is. 4. Check whether the comparison is fair For ML experiments, control the conditions as much as reasonably possible. Suppose: Model A Dataset: 100,000 samples Augmentation: yes Hyperparameter tuning: extensive Model B Dataset: 20,000 samples Augmentation: no Default hyperparameters Then a comparison between A and B is difficult to interpret. Ask: Same dataset? Same preprocessing? Same train/test split? Comparable tuning effort? Comparable training budget? Same evaluation metrics? Same access to external information? This is sometimes called apples-to-apples comparison. 5. Examine the dataset Dataset quality strongly affects experimental validity. Check: Size Is the dataset large enough for the proposed analysis? Representativeness Does it represent the population or environment the authors claim to address? Diversity Does it contain sufficient variation? Class balance Are some classes severely underrepresented? Data source Is it: synthetic? public benchmark? single institution? multiple institutions? real-world deployment data? A model can achieve excellent benchmark performance without necessarily being reliable in a different real-world environment. 6. Check the train/test split This is one of the most important checks in ML. Ask: Was the test set genuinely independent of the training process? Potential problems include: duplicate samples across train and test; data from the same person in both sets; temporal leakage; preprocessing performed using the entire dataset; test-set information used for hyperparameter tuning. For example, if images from the same patient appear in both training and test sets, the model may effectively see patient-specific information during training. The reported test performance may therefore overstate generalization. 7. Look for data leakage Data leakage occurs when information that should be unavailable during prediction enters the training process. Examples: Incorrect: Entire dataset ↓ Normalization/statistics ↓ Train/test split A safer procedure for many settings is: Dataset ↓ Train / Test split ↓ Fit preprocessing on training data ↓ Apply same transformation to test data Other leakage examples include: target-derived features; future information; test-set hyperparameter tuning; duplicate records; patient-level leakage. Data leakage can seriously undermine internal validity. 8. Evaluate the sample size Ask whether the amount of data supports the claims. For ML: How many training examples? How many test examples? How many examples per class? How many parameters does the model have? Is the test set large enough to estimate performance reliably? For user studies: How many participants? How were they recruited? Is the sample appropriate for the population being studied? A small sample isn't automatically invalid, but the claims should be appropriately limited. 9. Examine randomization Where appropriate, determine whether assignment was randomized. For example, in a user experiment: Participants are randomly assigned to either the AI-assisted or non-AI condition. Randomization can reduce systematic differences between groups. In ML, randomness can also affect: train/test splits; initialization; minibatch ordering; augmentation; hyperparameter search. Check whether random seeds and repeated experiments are reported. 10. Check whether the evaluation metrics are appropriate A paper can have a perfectly executed experiment but still use an inappropriate metric. For imbalanced classification: Accuracy alone may hide poor minority-class performance. You might need: precision; recall; F1; balanced accuracy; ROC-AUC; PR-AUC; sensitivity/specificity. For regression: MAE; RMSE; R2. The metric should correspond to the actual research objective. 11. Examine statistical uncertainty Don't focus only on a point estimate. Suppose: Model A: 91.2% accuracy Model B: 91.7% accuracy The difference is only 0.5 percentage points. Ask: Is that difference larger than the uncertainty associated with the experiment? Look for: confidence intervals; standard deviations; repeated runs; statistical tests where appropriate; effect sizes. For ML, reporting only the best run can be particularly misleading when training is stochastic. 12. Distinguish statistical significance from practical significance Suppose a paper finds: Model A improves accuracy from 95.0% to 95.1%, with a statistically detectable difference. That doesn't automatically mean the improvement is practically important. Ask: Is the size of the improvement meaningful for the intended application? Conversely, a practically meaningful difference might fail to reach conventional statistical significance because the study has limited statistical power. Both dimensions matter. 13. Examine the ablation study For complex ML models, an ablation study can reveal which components actually matter. Suppose the proposed architecture contains: CNN + Attention + Data augmentation + Special loss function The paper should ideally investigate components individually where appropriate: ConfigurationF1CNN0.87CNN + attention0.89CNN + augmentation0.90CNN + attention + augmentation0.92 This helps determine whether the claimed contribution actually produces the improvement. Without suitable ablations, it may be difficult to identify which component caused the reported effect. 14. Examine hyperparameter tuning A subtle problem is unequal optimization. Suppose the proposed model receives extensive hyperparameter tuning while the baseline uses default settings. Then: Proposed model = tuned Baseline = untuned is not necessarily a fair comparison. Ask: How were hyperparameters selected? Was a validation set used? Was the test set kept untouched? Did all models receive comparable tuning effort? How large was the search space? 15. Check for multiple comparisons and overfitting to the test set If researchers repeatedly evaluate many models on the same test set and choose the best one, the test set is gradually becoming part of the development process. Conceptually: Train ↓ Validate ↓ Modify model ↓ Test ↓ Modify model again ↓ Test again ↓ Choose best result This can make the final test performance overly optimistic. A genuinely held-out test set should ideally remain untouched until the final evaluation. 16. Examine external validity Internal validity asks: Is the reported effect credible under the experimental conditions? External validity asks: Does it generalize beyond those conditions? For an ML paper, examine: different datasets; different institutions; different geographic regions; different time periods; different hardware; different input distributions; real-world rather than benchmark data. For example: A model trained and tested on one hospital's data may not necessarily perform similarly at another hospital. External validation provides evidence about generalization, but its absence does not by itself invalidate a study; it limits what can reasonably be claimed. 17. Check whether the conclusions match the evidence This is perhaps the most important final step. Suppose the experiment shows: Model A performs better than Model B on Dataset X. The paper concludes: "Model A is superior for medical image classification." That conclusion is broader than the evidence. A more defensible conclusion might be: "Model A achieved higher performance than Model B under the experimental conditions evaluated on Dataset X." Ask: Is the conclusion no broader than the evidence supports? Watch for words such as: proves; always; superior; universally; guarantees; generalizes; causes. These require particularly strong evidence. 18. Assess reproducibility Experimental validity and reproducibility are related but different. Check whether the paper provides: source code; dataset information; preprocessing procedures; hyperparameters; train/test splits; random seeds; software versions; hardware; evaluation code. A paper can have a valid design but poor reproducibility because implementation details are missing. 19. Use a validity checklist You can evaluate each paper using: CriterionQuestionsAssessmentResearch questionDoes the experiment answer the stated question?VariablesAre variables clearly defined?ControlsAre relevant factors controlled?BaselineIs the comparison appropriate?DatasetIs the data appropriate and sufficiently described?SamplingIs the sample appropriate?Data splitIs test data genuinely independent?LeakageCould information leak between stages?MetricsAre evaluation measures appropriate?StatisticsIs uncertainty reported appropriately?Repeated runsIs stochastic variation addressed?AblationAre key components isolated?HyperparametersIs tuning fair and properly separated from testing?External validityIs generalization investigated?ReproducibilityCan the experiment be recreated?ConclusionsDo claims match the evidence? You can use Yes / Partial / No / Not applicable, followed by a short justification. 20. Write a critical evaluation Instead of saying: "The experimental design is good." write something like: The study uses a clearly defined test set and compares the proposed model with several established baselines under the same dataset and evaluation metric. However, hyperparameter-selection procedures are not fully described, and the authors do not report results across multiple random seeds. In addition, evaluation is limited to a single dataset, so the evidence for cross-dataset generalization is limited. The reported improvement should therefore be interpreted as evidence of better performance under the evaluated conditions rather than broad evidence of superiority. That is a critical evaluation because it connects specific design features to the strength and limits of the conclusions. A useful mental model Think of validity as a chain: Research question ↓ Appropriate experimental design? ↓ Appropriate data? ↓ Fair comparison? ↓ No leakage? ↓ Appropriate measurement? ↓ Sound statistical analysis? ↓ Robust results? ↓ Generalizable evidence? ↓ Conclusion supported? If one link is weak, identify exactly what claim it affects. The goal isn't to label a paper simply "valid" or "invalid." A stronger critical review says: What does the experiment establish with reasonable confidence, what does it not establish, and which design limitations explain that boundary?

prompt: Explain how to identify state-of-the-art benchmarks and baselines for a research topic.
chatgpt_response: Identifying state-of-the-art (SOTA) benchmarks and baselines means determining what methods are currently considered strong reference points for your specific research problem, dataset, and evaluation setting. For machine-learning research, this is more subtle than simply finding the paper with the highest reported accuracy. 1. First define exactly what you are benchmarking "SOTA" is always relative to a particular setting. Specify: Task: classification, detection, generation, retrieval, etc. Dataset: which benchmark? Metric: accuracy, F1, BLEU, mAP, RMSE, etc. Data split: which train/validation/test split? Time period: as of when? Constraints: accuracy only, or also latency, memory, compute, etc.? For example: "State of the art for image classification" is too broad. A more precise definition is: "Best reported F1-score for binary diabetic-retinopathy classification on Dataset X's official test split as of September 2026." That gives you something you can actually investigate. 2. Understand the difference between a benchmark and a baseline These terms are related but not identical. Benchmark A benchmark is a standardized task, dataset, evaluation protocol, or collection of tasks used to compare methods. Example: ImageNet classification using the official evaluation protocol. Baseline A baseline is a reference method against which your proposed method is compared. For example: Simple baseline → Logistic Regression Classical ML → Random Forest Deep-learning baseline → ResNet Modern baseline → Vision Transformer Proposed method → Your model A benchmark tells you where/how to evaluate. A baseline tells you what to compare against. 3. Start with benchmark papers and dataset papers Search for the original or widely recognized paper introducing the dataset or benchmark. Look for: dataset description; official evaluation protocol; baseline models; recommended metrics; standard train/test splits; benchmark leaderboards, if available. This gives you the reference experimental setting. For example, if a dataset has an official test split, using that split is generally more informative than inventing a new split and comparing your number with published results from a different protocol. 4. Search recent literature Because "state of the art" changes, you need current literature. For a current review, search combinations such as: [task] state of the art [dataset] benchmark [dataset] leaderboard [task] recent methods [task] benchmark comparison [dataset] transformer [task] 2025 2026 Then inspect recent papers and their comparison tables. For rapidly changing ML areas, conference proceedings and recent preprints can matter substantially, but distinguish peer-reviewed publications from preprints when reporting the evidence. 5. Follow the citation chain A particularly effective strategy is: Original benchmark ↓ Important baseline paper ↓ Recent papers citing it ↓ Latest competing methods ↓ Most recent benchmark comparisons For example: Find the dataset paper. Find the original benchmark results. Find influential methods that became common baselines. Examine newer papers that compare against those methods. Identify the strongest recent methods under the same evaluation protocol. This is often more reliable than searching only for "SOTA." 6. Look for benchmark tables Research papers frequently contain tables like: MethodDatasetAccuracyF1AUCMethod ADataset X91.290.594.1Method BDataset X93.492.895.7Method CDataset X94.193.696.2ProposedDataset X95.094.496.8 These tables are useful, but don't automatically accept the largest number as SOTA. Check whether all results were obtained under comparable conditions. 7. Check whether the datasets and splits are identical This is one of the biggest sources of misleading SOTA comparisons. Suppose: Paper A: 96% accuracy on Dataset X and: Paper B: 97% accuracy on Dataset X + external data Those aren't necessarily equivalent experiments. Likewise: Paper A: official test set Paper B: random 80/20 split The numbers shouldn't simply be placed in the same ranking. Always check: dataset version; training data; additional data; test split; preprocessing; external data; augmentation. 8. Check the evaluation metric A method isn't necessarily SOTA because it has the highest accuracy. For an imbalanced classification task, for example: Model A: 98% accuracy, F1 = 72% Model B: 95% accuracy, F1 = 89% Depending on the research objective, F1 may be much more informative than accuracy. Identify the primary metric appropriate to the benchmark. Then compare methods using that metric. 9. Check whether external data was used This is a particularly important SOTA issue. Imagine: Method A Uses only the benchmark training set. Method B Uses benchmark training data + millions of additional samples. Method B may report a higher score, but it is not necessarily a fair comparison if your research constraint is training only on the benchmark dataset. Therefore record: MethodBenchmark data only?External data?AYesNoBNoYesCYesNo This distinction can completely change which methods are appropriate baselines. 10. Separate architecture from training recipe Modern ML performance often depends on much more than the model architecture. Compare: pretrained weights; training data; augmentation; optimizer; learning-rate schedule; loss function; test-time augmentation; ensembling; model size; training duration. For example, saying: "Transformer beats CNN" may be misleading if the transformer used substantially more pretraining data and compute. A good benchmark comparison isolates these differences where possible. 11. Identify different categories of baselines For a strong experiment, you often want several kinds of baselines. 1. Simple baseline A straightforward method. Examples: Logistic Regression Linear Regression Decision Tree majority-class classifier Purpose: Establish a minimum reference point. 2. Classical ML baseline Examples: Random Forest SVM XGBoost Purpose: Determine whether the proposed deep-learning method provides meaningful improvement over established approaches. 3. Strong deep-learning baseline Examples: ResNet EfficientNet BERT standard Transformer Purpose: Compare against a recognized modern architecture. 4. Current SOTA baseline The strongest relevant recent method under comparable conditions. Purpose: Determine whether your contribution improves upon current research. 5. Ablation baseline Your own model with one component removed. Example: Full model vs. Full model − attention vs. Full model − augmentation vs. Full model − auxiliary loss Purpose: Determine which components contribute to the result. 12. Use leaderboards carefully If an official benchmark leaderboard exists, it can be very useful. But check: whether submissions use the same test set; whether external training data is allowed; whether the leaderboard has changed over time; whether results are independently verified; whether entries are peer-reviewed; whether the metric definition has changed. A leaderboard entry is evidence of benchmark performance, but it doesn't necessarily tell you everything about methodological quality or reproducibility. 13. Identify the "true" baseline for your research question Suppose you're proposing: A lightweight CNN for edge-device image classification. The most relevant baseline isn't necessarily the model with the highest accuracy. You might need to compare against models with similar deployment constraints: ModelAccuracyParametersLatencyModel A96%25M100 msModel B94%5M30 msProposed95%3M15 ms If your research question concerns efficient edge inference, Model B may be a particularly relevant baseline even though Model A has higher accuracy. Thus: Relevant baseline ≠ highest-performing model. 14. Check how recent "SOTA" claims are A paper published in 2021 may state: "We achieve state-of-the-art performance." That means SOTA at the time of that paper, not necessarily today. When reviewing the literature, attach a date: "The paper reported SOTA performance on Dataset X as of 2021." Then search for later work. This prevents outdated SOTA claims from being treated as current facts. 15. Watch for incomparable results Suppose you find: PaperScoreA95.2B96.1C97.4 You might think C is SOTA. But after investigation: A uses Dataset X; B uses Dataset X + external data; C uses a different test split. Then the table isn't a valid SOTA ranking. A good literature review might instead say: The reported results cannot be directly ranked because the studies use different data sources and evaluation protocols. Recognizing non-comparability is itself an important research skill. 16. Search for benchmark saturation Sometimes a benchmark has become saturated. You might find: 95.2 → 95.8 → 96.0 → 96.1 → 96.2 Over several years. At that point, a tiny numerical improvement may not represent a meaningful scientific contribution. Look for alternative evaluation dimensions: robustness; calibration; fairness; efficiency; out-of-distribution performance; external validation; interpretability; data efficiency. This can reveal more interesting research directions than chasing another 0.1% on a saturated benchmark. 17. Create a SOTA tracking table For your literature review, maintain something like: PaperYearDatasetData UsedMethodMetricScoreExternal DataCodeComparable?A2022XBenchmarkCNNF10.91NoYesYesB2023XBenchmarkTransformerF10.93NoYesYesC2024XBenchmark + externalHybridF10.96YesPartialNoD2026XBenchmarkNew modelF10.95NoYesYes Now you can distinguish: highest reported score highest comparable score strongest reproducible baseline strongest baseline under your experimental constraints These may be different methods. 18. Define your baseline set before running experiments For a research project, don't decide afterward which models you want to compare against. Before experimentation, establish: Minimum baseline A simple established method. Strong baseline A recognized modern method. Current relevant SOTA A recent method appropriate to your exact benchmark setting. Proposed method Your approach. For example: Logistic Regression ↓ Random Forest ↓ ResNet ↓ Vision Transformer ↓ Recent SOTA method ↓ Your proposed method The exact models depend on the research topic. 19. The most important question When you find a paper claiming SOTA, ask: "SOTA under exactly what conditions?" Then document: Task: Dataset: Dataset version: Train/test split: Metric: External data: Pretraining: Model: Additional techniques: Publication date: Code availability: Only after answering these should you treat the result as a relevant benchmark. A practical workflow Define your exact task ↓ Identify the standard benchmark ↓ Find the benchmark/dataset paper ↓ Find established baseline methods ↓ Search recent literature ↓ Follow citation chains ↓ Collect benchmark tables ↓ Verify dataset + split + metric ↓ Check external data/pretraining ↓ Check reproducibility ↓ Identify comparable recent methods ↓ Select appropriate baselines ↓ Document everything in a benchmark table Bottom line Don't define SOTA as simply "the paper with the biggest number." Define it as: The strongest documented performance for the specific task, dataset, evaluation protocol, and constraints relevant to your study, while accounting for differences in data, training resources, and experimental methodology. That distinction is crucial when designing a credible computer-science experiment.

prompt: Explain how to conduct a systematic literature review using the PRISMA framework.
chatgpt_response: A systematic literature review (SLR) is a structured way to find, select, evaluate, and synthesize all relevant research addressing a clearly defined question. PRISMA provides a reporting framework that helps you transparently document how you identified, screened, and included studies. For computer science and machine learning, PRISMA is especially useful when you want your literature review to be systematic, reproducible, and defensible rather than simply descriptive. 1. Understand what PRISMA is PRISMA stands for Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. It mainly helps you report: how you searched for studies; which databases you searched; how many records you found; how duplicates were removed; how studies were screened; why studies were excluded; which studies were finally included; how the included studies were analyzed. A simplified PRISMA workflow is: Identification ↓ Records found through databases ↓ Duplicate removal ↓ Screening ↓ Title/abstract screening ↓ Full-text eligibility assessment ↓ Included ↓ Final studies in systematic review Importantly, PRISMA is primarily a reporting guideline, not a complete research methodology by itself. Your SLR still needs a clearly designed search strategy, eligibility criteria, quality assessment, and synthesis method. 2. Define your research question Start with a focused research question. For example: "How effective are deep-learning methods for detecting diabetic retinopathy from retinal images?" You can break this into components such as: ComponentExamplePopulation/dataRetinal imagesInterventionDeep-learning methodsComparisonTraditional ML/deep-learning baselinesOutcomeClassification performanceContextDiabetic retinopathy detection For quantitative questions, frameworks such as PICO can help: P — Population/problem I — Intervention C — Comparison O — Outcome For other types of CS questions, other question frameworks may be more appropriate. 3. Define a review protocol Before searching extensively, create a review protocol. The protocol specifies what you intend to do. Include: research questions; databases; search terms; publication period; inclusion criteria; exclusion criteria; screening procedure; quality-assessment method; data-extraction fields; synthesis method. For example: Research question: What deep-learning methods have been used for retinal disease detection? Databases: IEEE Xplore ACM Digital Library Scopus Web of Science PubMed Google Scholar Publication period: 2018–2026 Language: English Study type: Peer-reviewed research articles and conference papers The protocol reduces the temptation to change the methodology after seeing the results. 4. Define inclusion and exclusion criteria This is one of the most important parts of an SLR. Example inclusion criteria Include studies that: address the target research problem; use machine-learning/deep-learning methods; evaluate the target outcome; provide experimental results; fall within the specified publication period; meet your publication-type requirements. Example exclusion criteria Exclude studies that: are unrelated to the research question; are duplicates; contain insufficient methodological information; are editorials or opinion pieces; do not provide experimental results; fall outside the specified period; use a different task or population. Put these rules in writing before screening. 5. Design your search strategy Develop search terms from the major concepts in your research question. Suppose the topic is: Deep learning for diabetic-retinopathy detection. You might construct: ("diabetic retinopathy" OR "retinal disease") AND ("deep learning" OR "neural network" OR "CNN" OR transformer) AND ("detection" OR "classification" OR screening) Use: synonyms; alternative spellings; abbreviations; related technical terms; Boolean operators. Example search structure Concept 1 (diabetic retinopathy OR retinal disease) AND Concept 2 (deep learning OR CNN OR neural network OR transformer) AND Concept 3 (detection OR classification OR screening) Don't use exactly the same query blindly in every database. Adapt syntax to each database's search capabilities. 6. Select appropriate databases Use multiple sources rather than relying on one search engine. For computer science/ML, potentially relevant sources include: IEEE Xplore ACM Digital Library Scopus Web of Science SpringerLink ScienceDirect PubMed for biomedical topics Google Scholar domain-specific repositories where appropriate The exact combination depends on your topic. Record: DatabaseSearch dateSearch queryResultsIEEE XploreDateQuery A320ACM DLDateQuery B180ScopusDateQuery C540PubMedDateQuery D210 This search log is important for reproducibility. 7. Run the searches and collect all records Export the search results whenever possible. Useful formats include: BibTeX RIS CSV EndNote Reference managers such as Zotero, EndNote, or similar tools can help organize the records. At this stage, don't aggressively remove studies just because they look irrelevant from a quick glance. First collect the records systematically. 8. Remove duplicate records The same paper may appear in multiple databases. For example: IEEE Xplore → 400 Scopus → 600 ACM → 250 PubMed → 300 ↓ Total records = 1,550 ↓ Duplicates removed = 420 ↓ Unique records = 1,130 Record the numbers because they will later appear in your PRISMA flow diagram. 9. Screen titles and abstracts Now perform the first screening stage. Read: title; abstract; keywords where necessary. Apply your predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria. For example: StudyRelevant topic?Correct method?Correct outcome?DecisionPaper AYesYesYesIncludePaper BNo——ExcludePaper CYesNo—ExcludePaper DYesYesYesInclude Record the reason for exclusion where appropriate. 10. Perform full-text screening For papers that pass the first screening, obtain and read the full text. Now ask more detailed questions: Does the study actually answer the review question? Does it satisfy all inclusion criteria? Is the methodology appropriate? Does it provide sufficient results? Is the study type eligible? Does it contain enough information for data extraction? For example: 1,550 records identified ↓ 420 duplicates removed ↓ 1,130 records screened ↓ 850 excluded based on title/abstract ↓ 280 full texts assessed ↓ 190 excluded ↓ 90 studies included The exact numbers are hypothetical; your actual review should report your real counts. 11. Record reasons for full-text exclusion Don't simply write: "Excluded after full-text review." Use specific reasons such as: wrong population; wrong task; wrong intervention; no experimental evaluation; insufficient data; duplicate publication; outside scope; inaccessible full text, if this is genuinely part of your eligibility process. This makes the review more transparent. 12. Assess the quality of included studies Not all published studies are equally reliable. Create a quality-assessment checklist appropriate to your field. For ML research, questions might include: CriterionQuestionDatasetIs the dataset clearly described?Data splitIs train/test separation clear?LeakageIs data leakage addressed?BaselineIs the comparison baseline appropriate?MetricsAre appropriate evaluation metrics reported?ReproducibilityIs sufficient implementation information provided?ValidationIs validation performed appropriately?StatisticsIs uncertainty/repeated experimentation reported?GeneralizationIs performance tested beyond one narrow setting?LimitationsAre limitations clearly discussed? You can classify each criterion as: Yes Partially No Unclear Avoid automatically treating a published paper as high quality simply because it appeared in a reputable venue. 13. Extract data systematically Create a standardized extraction table. For an ML systematic review, useful fields include: FieldExampleAuthor/yearSmith et al., 2024Research objectiveDisease classificationDatasetDataset XDataset size50,000 imagesPreprocessingResizing + normalizationModelCNNBaselineResNetTraining strategyTransfer learningEvaluation5-fold CVMetricsF1, AUCResultsF1 = 0.91External validationNoCode availableYesLimitationsSingle datasetResearch gapLimited generalization Use the same extraction fields for every included study. 14. Synthesize the evidence This is where an SLR becomes more than a collection of summaries. Look for patterns across the studies. Methodological patterns For example: Most studies use CNN-based architectures, while relatively few evaluate transformer-based methods. Dataset patterns Most studies rely on the same public dataset, with limited external validation. Evaluation patterns Accuracy is frequently reported, whereas calibration and robustness are rarely evaluated. Reproducibility patterns Many papers describe the architecture but do not provide training configurations or source code. These patterns can lead directly to research gaps. 15. Use quantitative synthesis when appropriate If studies report sufficiently comparable numerical results, you may perform quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis. For example: Study A → F1 = 0.88 Study B → F1 = 0.91 Study C → F1 = 0.89 Study D → F1 = 0.93 However, don't statistically combine results merely because they report the same metric. Check whether they have sufficiently comparable: populations; datasets; interventions; outcome definitions; experimental designs. For many computer-science SLRs, a structured narrative synthesis is more appropriate because models, datasets, protocols, and metrics vary substantially. 16. Construct the PRISMA flow diagram Your final review should show the movement of studies through the review process. A simplified structure is: IDENTIFICATION │ Records identified from databases/other sources │ ▼ Duplicate records removed │ ▼ SCREENING │ Titles/abstracts screened │ ▼ Records excluded │ ▼ ELIGIBILITY │ Full-text reports assessed │ ▼ Full-text reports excluded + reasons for exclusion │ ▼ INCLUDED │ Studies included in systematic review PRISMA provides standardized reporting for this process. 17. Write the review A typical SLR structure is: 1. Introduction Explain: research problem; importance; existing literature; motivation for the review; review objectives/questions. 2. Methodology Describe: PRISMA framework; research questions; databases; search strategy; search dates; eligibility criteria; screening procedure; quality assessment; data extraction; synthesis method. 3. Results Report: number of identified studies; screening results; included studies; study characteristics; methodological trends; datasets; algorithms; performance; quality assessment. 4. Discussion Interpret the patterns: What approaches dominate? What findings are consistent? Where are results contradictory? What methodological weaknesses recur? What research gaps remain? 5. Limitations Discuss limitations of your review: database coverage; language restrictions; publication bias; search-term limitations; heterogeneity between studies; inaccessible studies. 6. Conclusion Summarize: what the evidence shows; major gaps; implications for future research. 18. Keep a complete audit trail A strong PRISMA-based review should allow another researcher to understand how you arrived at your final set of papers. Keep: Research protocol ↓ Search strings ↓ Database list ↓ Search dates ↓ Raw search results ↓ Duplicate-removal records ↓ Screening decisions ↓ Full-text exclusions + reasons ↓ Quality assessments ↓ Data-extraction sheet ↓ Final included studies This is one of the major differences between a systematic review and an informal literature review. Example: Complete PRISMA workflow for an ML study Suppose your topic is: Deep learning for cybersecurity intrusion detection Your workflow might be: Research question "What deep-learning approaches are used for network intrusion detection, and how are they evaluated?" ↓ Define inclusion/exclusion criteria ↓ Build search query ↓ Search IEEE + ACM + Scopus + Web of Science ↓ Export results ↓ Remove duplicates ↓ Title/abstract screening ↓ Full-text screening ↓ Quality assessment ↓ Data extraction ↓ Compare: • datasets • architectures • preprocessing • baselines • metrics • validation • reproducibility ↓ Synthesize evidence ↓ Identify research gaps ↓ Report using PRISMA PRISMA checklist for your own SLR Before submitting your review, check: Research design Research questions clearly defined Review protocol established Inclusion criteria defined Exclusion criteria defined Search Multiple appropriate databases searched Search strings documented Search dates recorded Search results saved Screening Duplicates removed systematically Titles/abstracts screened Full texts assessed Exclusion reasons recorded Quality Quality-assessment criteria defined Studies assessed consistently Extraction Standard extraction form used Dataset/method/results extracted Limitations recorded Synthesis Studies grouped into meaningful themes Results compared appropriately Heterogeneity considered Research gaps supported by evidence Reporting PRISMA flow diagram included Search strategy reported Study-selection process reported Included studies described Limitations of the review discussed The key distinction An ordinary literature review often looks like: Find papers → read papers → summarize papers → identify gaps. A PRISMA-oriented systematic review is more like: Define question → establish protocol → search systematically → remove duplicates → screen → assess eligibility → assess quality → extract data → synthesize evidence → report transparently. The central principle is transparency and reproducibility: another researcher should be able to understand not only what papers you included, but how and why you arrived at that set of papers.

prompt: Explain how to turn a literature survey into a well-defined research proposal.
chatgpt_response: Turning a literature survey into a research proposal means moving from: “Here is what other researchers have done.” to: “Here is what is still missing, why it matters, what I will investigate, and how I will investigate it.” The literature survey provides the evidence and justification for the proposal. The proposal converts that evidence into a concrete research plan. 1. Start with the literature, not with a solution After reviewing the literature, summarize the current state of knowledge. For example, suppose your topic is: Deep learning for medical image classification. Your survey may show: CNNs are widely used. Transformer-based models are increasingly being explored. Most studies use one or two public datasets. Many report accuracy and F1. Few studies perform external validation. Training configurations are inconsistently reported. Generalization to unseen datasets remains unclear. Don't immediately jump to: "I will develop a new hybrid CNN-transformer." First ask: What problem in the existing evidence actually requires investigation? 2. Convert observations into a research gap A literature survey may reveal many observations, but not all are research gaps. For example: Observation "Most papers use CNNs." This alone isn't necessarily a research gap. Stronger gap "Although CNN-based models perform well on individual benchmark datasets, relatively few studies evaluate whether their performance generalizes to independently collected datasets using a standardized evaluation protocol." Now you have: What is known: CNNs perform well on benchmark datasets. What is unclear: Whether performance generalizes across datasets. Why it matters: High performance on one dataset may not indicate robust real-world performance. This is much closer to a proposal-worthy problem. 3. Build a gap-to-proposal chain A useful structure is: Literature ↓ What is already known? ↓ What is missing? ↓ Why does the missing part matter? ↓ Research problem ↓ Research objective ↓ Research questions ↓ Hypotheses, if appropriate ↓ Methodology ↓ Expected contribution Every stage should logically follow from the previous one. 4. Write the problem statement The problem statement explains what is wrong, unknown, or insufficiently understood. A strong problem statement usually contains four parts: 1. Context What area are you studying? 2. Current knowledge What has previous research established? 3. Gap What remains unresolved? 4. Consequence Why is that unresolved issue important? For example: Deep-learning models have achieved strong performance in medical image classification, particularly on widely used public datasets. However, existing studies frequently evaluate models using a single dataset and heterogeneous experimental protocols. Consequently, it remains unclear whether reported performance differences reflect genuine model improvements or differences in data preparation, training procedures, and evaluation settings. A systematic comparison under a standardized cross-dataset protocol is therefore needed. Notice that the paragraph doesn't simply say: "Nobody has studied this." Instead, it explains what is known, what is unclear, and why the uncertainty matters. 5. Turn the gap into a research objective The objective describes what your study will actually do. For example: Objective: To systematically evaluate the generalization performance of deep-learning models across independent medical-image datasets using a standardized experimental protocol. A good objective contains: Action + subject + context/purpose Common action verbs include: investigate; evaluate; compare; characterize; analyze; develop; validate; determine; assess. Avoid vague objectives such as: "To study deep learning." 6. Formulate research questions Now turn the objective into specific questions. For example: Main RQ RQ1: How does the performance of different deep-learning architectures change when evaluated across independent datasets? Supporting RQs RQ2: Which architectural characteristics are associated with better cross-dataset generalization? RQ3: How do preprocessing and training strategies influence cross-dataset performance? RQ4: How does cross-dataset performance compare with conventional within-dataset evaluation? Notice the progression: Research gap ↓ Objective ↓ Research questions The RQs should directly address the gap identified in the literature survey. 7. Decide whether hypotheses are appropriate If your study is experimental and tests specific effects, formulate hypotheses. For example: H1: Models trained using the proposed domain-generalization strategy achieve higher cross-dataset F1 scores than models trained without the strategy under the same experimental conditions. H0: There is no statistically detectable difference in cross-dataset F1 between the two conditions. But don't force hypotheses into every proposal. Exploratory, qualitative, descriptive, or design-oriented studies may be better served by research questions alone. 8. Define the variables Your literature survey should help you determine what needs to be measured. For an ML experiment: Independent variables Things you manipulate or compare: model architecture; training strategy; augmentation; feature representation; amount of training data. Dependent variables Things you measure: accuracy; precision; recall; F1; AUC; latency; memory usage. Control variables Things kept consistent: dataset split; preprocessing; training budget; evaluation metric; hardware where appropriate; randomization protocol. This makes the proposal experimentally precise. 9. Design the methodology from the research questions A common mistake is: "I want to use CNN + Transformer, so I'll make that my research proposal." Instead, the methodology should follow the research question. For example: RQ: Does the proposed approach improve cross-dataset generalization? Then the methodology needs: Dataset A ↓ Training ↓ Model ↓ Dataset B ↓ External evaluation ↓ Compare with baselines You need an experimental design capable of actually answering the RQ. 10. Select datasets Explain: what datasets will be used; why they are appropriate; sample sizes; classes; data sources; train/validation/test splits; inclusion/exclusion criteria; whether external datasets will be used. For an ML proposal, explicitly state whether the test set will remain untouched during model selection. 11. Select meaningful baselines Your literature survey should identify established methods that your proposed approach needs to be compared against. For example: Simple baseline ↓ Classical ML baseline ↓ Established deep-learning baseline ↓ Recent strong/SOTA baseline ↓ Proposed method Don't choose baselines merely because they are easy to implement. Ask: Which existing methods would a knowledgeable researcher expect to see in this comparison? 12. Define the evaluation protocol Specify: evaluation metrics; validation strategy; number of experimental runs; random seeds; confidence intervals or variability measures where appropriate; statistical comparisons where appropriate; computational cost; external validation; ablation studies. For example: Models will be evaluated using macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and AUROC. Each experiment will be repeated using multiple random seeds, and mean performance with variability estimates will be reported. This is much stronger than simply saying: "The model will be evaluated using accuracy." 13. Connect every methodological decision to the literature The literature survey shouldn't disappear after the introduction. Use it to justify your choices. For example: Previous studies predominantly report accuracy, despite class imbalance in the target datasets. Therefore, this study will additionally report macro-F1 and balanced accuracy. Or: Existing studies frequently evaluate models using random splits of a single dataset. To address the identified generalization gap, this study will use an independent dataset for external evaluation. This demonstrates that your methodology is derived from the research gap. 14. Define the expected contribution A research proposal should explain what it intends to contribute. Possible contribution types include: Methodological contribution A new training or modeling approach. Empirical contribution A systematic comparison under standardized conditions. Dataset contribution A new dataset or benchmark. Evaluation contribution A new evaluation protocol. Theoretical contribution New understanding of why a particular method works. Practical contribution Improved efficiency, robustness, interpretability, or deployment performance. Not every proposal needs a new algorithm. A carefully designed empirical study can make a meaningful contribution if it resolves an important uncertainty. 15. Distinguish novelty from implementation This is particularly important in computer science. Suppose you propose: "Use a Vision Transformer for Dataset X." That may not be sufficient novelty if Vision Transformers have already been extensively evaluated for the same task. But: "Evaluate whether Vision Transformers generalize better than CNNs across three independently collected datasets under a standardized training and evaluation protocol" could address a specific empirical gap. Your proposal should therefore answer: What is new about this study relative to existing work? 16. State the scope clearly A proposal becomes much stronger when its boundaries are explicit. For example: Included: three public datasets; three model families; image classification; supervised learning; standardized preprocessing. Not included: segmentation; object detection; multimodal learning; clinical deployment; real-time inference. This prevents the project from becoming unrealistically broad. 17. Build a conceptual framework You can represent the research logic visually: Literature Survey │ ▼ Research Gap │ ▼ Research Problem │ ▼ Research Objective │ ▼ Research Questions │ ┌──────────┴──────────┐ ▼ ▼ Hypotheses Variables │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ▼ Methodology │ ▼ Experiments │ ▼ Evaluation │ ▼ Findings │ ▼ Contribution This is the logical backbone of the proposal. 18. Use a literature-to-proposal matrix This is one of the most useful tools for converting a survey into a proposal. Literature findingLimitation/gapResearch questionProposed methodExpected contributionCNNs perform strongly on Dataset ALimited cross-dataset validationRQ1Train/test across independent datasetsEvidence about generalizationStudies use different preprocessingComparisons may be unfairRQ2Standardized preprocessingFair benchmarkAccuracy is dominant metricImbalance insufficiently addressedRQ3F1 + balanced metricsMore robust evaluationFew studies report multiple runsVariability unclearRQ4Multiple seedsReliability estimates This table makes the transformation from literature survey → research proposal explicit. 19. Structure the final research proposal A typical computer-science research proposal can be organized as follows: 1. Title Specific and informative. 2. Background Introduce the research area. 3. Literature review Summarize the relevant evidence. 4. Research gap Clearly identify what remains unresolved. 5. Problem statement Define the specific problem your research addresses. 6. Aim/objective State what the study will accomplish. 7. Research questions List the questions your study will answer. 8. Hypotheses Include them where appropriate. 9. Methodology Describe: datasets; preprocessing; models; baselines; experimental design; evaluation; statistical analysis. 10. Expected contribution Explain what new knowledge or capability the research will provide. 11. Scope and limitations Define boundaries and anticipated limitations. 12. Timeline Break the project into stages. 13. References Include the literature supporting the problem, gap, methodology, and proposed contribution. 20. A complete example Suppose your literature survey finds: Existing papers report high accuracy for deep-learning models on individual cybersecurity datasets. However, studies use different preprocessing procedures, data splits, and metrics, and relatively few evaluate models across independent datasets. You can transform this into: Research problem The lack of standardized and cross-dataset evaluation makes it difficult to determine whether reported improvements in intrusion-detection models represent genuine improvements in generalization. Objective To systematically compare deep-learning approaches for network intrusion detection using standardized experimental and cross-dataset evaluation protocols. Research question How do different deep-learning architectures compare in their ability to generalize across independently collected intrusion-detection datasets? Hypothesis Under a standardized evaluation protocol, model architectures will differ significantly in their cross-dataset generalization performance. Methodology Datasets ↓ Common preprocessing ↓ Multiple baseline architectures ↓ Proposed/selected method ↓ Within-dataset evaluation ↓ Cross-dataset evaluation ↓ Multiple runs ↓ Statistical comparison ↓ Error/generalization analysis Expected contribution A standardized empirical comparison that clarifies the relationship between within-dataset performance and cross-dataset generalization. Notice that the proposal emerged directly from the literature findings. The most important principle A strong research proposal should have a traceable chain of reasoning: Literature → Gap → Problem → Objective → Research Questions → Method → Evaluation → Contribution If you cannot explain how one step leads to the next, the proposal probably needs refinement. A useful final test is to ask five questions: What do we already know? What don't we know? Why does that missing knowledge matter? What exactly will this study investigate? How will the proposed experiment provide evidence to answer it? If your literature survey provides convincing answers to the first three and your proposal provides precise answers to the last two, you have the foundation of a well-defined research proposal.

prompt: Compare survey papers and original research papers and how to use each in your work.
chatgpt_response: Survey papers and original research papers serve different purposes in academic research. A strong literature review usually needs both: survey papers help you understand the field, while original papers provide the primary evidence you cite and analyze. 1. Basic difference AspectSurvey/Review PaperOriginal Research PaperMain purposeSummarizes existing researchReports new researchPrimary contributionSynthesis of existing knowledgeNew method, experiment, dataset, theory, or findingDataUsually analyzes published studiesCollects or uses experimental dataResearch questionOften broadUsually specificResultsSynthesized from previous studiesProduced by the authors' own studyBest useUnderstand the fieldSupport specific claims and evidenceTypical roleMap the research landscapeProvide primary evidenceExample"A survey of deep-learning methods for intrusion detection""A new transformer model for intrusion detection" 2. What is a survey paper? A survey paper systematically organizes and discusses existing research in a particular area. For example: "A Survey of Deep Learning for Network Intrusion Detection" might examine: CNN-based methods; RNN-based methods; transformers; datasets; evaluation metrics; challenges; research gaps. It may compare dozens or hundreds of papers. A survey is therefore useful for answering: "What has been studied in this field?" 3. What is an original research paper? An original research paper presents research conducted by the authors. For example: "A Transformer-Based Approach for Network Intrusion Detection" might introduce: a new architecture; a new training strategy; a new dataset; new experiments; comparisons with baselines; new empirical findings. It answers a more specific question such as: "Does this proposed approach improve intrusion detection under these experimental conditions?" 4. Survey papers are excellent for getting started When entering an unfamiliar research area, reading a few good surveys can save considerable time. A survey can help you discover: Survey paper ↓ Major research themes ↓ Important datasets ↓ Common methods ↓ Important papers ↓ Research gaps ↓ Original research papers For example, if you're new to federated learning, a survey might introduce: FedAvg; FedProx; communication-efficient methods; privacy mechanisms; benchmark datasets; common evaluation metrics. You can then locate the original papers behind those methods. 5. But don't rely entirely on survey papers A common mistake is: Find one survey → use its references → write the entire literature review from the survey. This can create several problems. The survey may: be outdated; omit recent research; interpret a study differently from the original authors; contain its own selection criteria; summarize results without all experimental details. Therefore, use surveys as a map, not as the entire evidence base. 6. Use original papers for important technical claims Suppose you write: "Method X achieved 94.2% F1 on Dataset Y." Ideally, cite the original paper reporting that result, not merely a survey that mentions it. Why? Because the original paper contains: experimental conditions; dataset details; preprocessing; baselines; evaluation metrics; statistical information; limitations. This allows you to verify exactly what the reported number means. 7. Use surveys to understand terminology and taxonomy Suppose your topic is: Explainable AI. A survey might organize approaches into: Explainable AI ├── Intrinsic methods ├── Post-hoc methods │ ├── Feature-based │ ├── Example-based │ └── Attribution-based ├── Model-specific └── Model-agnostic This gives you a conceptual structure for your literature review. You can then investigate important original papers within each category. 8. Use original papers to understand methods deeply A survey might tell you: "Several studies use attention mechanisms for interpretability." But the original research paper can tell you: exactly how attention was implemented; which architecture was used; how it was trained; which datasets were used; what baseline was used; what the results actually demonstrated. For technical research, this distinction is important. 9. Use surveys to identify research gaps Survey papers often contain sections such as: limitations; open challenges; future directions; unresolved problems; research opportunities. These are useful starting points. But don't automatically treat: "Future work should investigate X" as an established research gap. Search for newer original research to determine whether someone has already addressed X. The process should be: Survey identifies possible gap ↓ Search recent papers ↓ Check whether gap still exists ↓ Compare existing attempts ↓ Define your research gap 10. Use original papers to verify whether a gap is real Suppose a 2022 survey says: "Few studies evaluate cross-dataset generalization." Before building a research proposal around this, search papers from 2023–2026. You may discover: several papers have already addressed it; only certain datasets have been studied; existing studies disagree; the problem remains unresolved under certain conditions. Your research gap should be based on the current body of evidence, not simply on an old survey's future-work section. 11. Use surveys to find influential papers A good survey can function like a research roadmap. Suppose you find: 2024 Survey of Vision Transformers It may identify: original Vision Transformer paper; major improvements; benchmark datasets; influential architectures; important comparative studies. You can then follow those citations. This is often much faster than trying to discover the field from scratch. 12. Use original papers for your comparison tables Suppose your thesis contains: MethodDatasetF1AccuracyYearMethod AX0.8891%2022Method BX0.9193%2023Method CX0.9495%2025 You should ideally obtain these values from the original research papers and record the experimental conditions. Don't assume that numbers copied from a survey are directly comparable. 13. Surveys are particularly useful for broad questions Use surveys when your question is: "What approaches exist?" "How has this field evolved?" "What are the major categories of methods?" "Which datasets are commonly used?" "What challenges have researchers identified?" Original papers are more useful for: "How does Method A work?" "What performance did Method A achieve?" "What dataset did the authors use?" "How was the experiment conducted?" "What evidence supports this specific claim?" 14. A useful hierarchy of sources For many research tasks, you can think of sources like this: Literature understanding │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ ↓ ↓ Survey papers Original papers ↓ ↓ Field structure Primary evidence Major methods Specific results Research themes Experimental details Important references Methodological evidence └───────────┬───────────┘ ↓ Your synthesis ↓ Research proposal You need both, but for different purposes. 15. Example: machine-learning research Suppose your research topic is: Deep learning for fake-news detection Step 1 — Find surveys A survey might tell you that the field contains: traditional ML; CNN/RNN approaches; transformer-based approaches; graph-based approaches; multimodal methods. You now understand the landscape. Step 2 — Find original papers You then select important papers representing these approaches. For each one, extract: PaperMethodDatasetFeaturesMetricResultLimitationASVMDataset XTF-IDFF10.82Limited contextBLSTMDataset XWord embeddingsF10.87Dataset-specificCBERTDataset XContextual embeddingsF10.91Computational costDGraph modelDataset YUser/content graphF10.93Requires graph information Now you're performing your own synthesis rather than simply repeating a survey. 16. Don't confuse different types of review papers Not every "review" paper is the same. You may encounter: Narrative review Provides a broad discussion of the literature. Systematic literature review Uses a predefined and transparent search/screening methodology. Systematic mapping study Maps research areas, methods, topics, or trends. Meta-analysis Statistically combines quantitative results from multiple studies when appropriate. Survey paper In computer science, often provides a structured overview/taxonomy of a research area, though the exact methodology varies. Check the paper's methodology rather than assuming every paper titled "survey" follows PRISMA or a systematic-review protocol. 17. How many of each should you use? There is no universal required ratio. A practical approach is: Early stage Use more surveys/reviews to understand the field. Developing your literature review Increase your use of original research papers. Writing technical claims Prefer the relevant original papers. Identifying current gaps Use recent original papers plus recent reviews/surveys. A thesis literature review should generally not consist primarily of summaries of a few survey papers. 18. Citation example Suppose a survey says: Transformer architectures have become increasingly common in NLP. You can cite the survey when discussing the broad trend. But if you write: "BERT achieved X on benchmark Y under experimental condition Z" you should consult and cite the original BERT research paper and the relevant benchmark evidence. The principle is: Use secondary sources to understand and organize; use primary sources to substantiate specific research claims. 19. Common mistakes Mistake 1: Using only survey papers Problem: Your review becomes second-hand knowledge. Better: Use surveys to discover original studies. Mistake 2: Citing a survey for every technical result Problem: You may lose important experimental context. Better: Cite the original study for specific results. Mistake 3: Treating survey "future work" as a guaranteed research gap Problem: The gap may have been addressed since publication. Better: Search newer original papers. Mistake 4: Copying a survey's taxonomy without evaluating it Problem: Different surveys may categorize methods differently. Better: Compare multiple sources and construct a taxonomy appropriate to your research question. Mistake 5: Comparing reported numbers without checking conditions Problem: Results may come from different datasets, splits, preprocessing, or metrics. Better: Verify the original experiments. 20. A practical workflow For a new research topic, you can use: 1. Find 3–5 strong recent surveys/reviews ↓ 2. Learn terminology and major research themes ↓ 3. Identify important datasets and benchmarks ↓ 4. Identify influential original papers ↓ 5. Search for recent original studies ↓ 6. Extract methods, datasets, experiments, and results ↓ 7. Compare studies under equivalent conditions ↓ 8. Identify limitations and contradictions ↓ 9. Determine whether proposed gaps are still open ↓ 10. Build your own synthesis and research gap The key idea Think of the two types of papers as serving different roles: Survey papers are your map of the research landscape. Original research papers are the evidence you investigate on that landscape. For a strong research project, use surveys to learn the field quickly and organize your thinking, then use original papers to verify claims, analyze methods, compare results, identify unresolved problems, and justify your own research proposal. prompt: Explain how pointers work in C with an example that modifies a variable through a function.
chatgpt_response:
A pointer in C is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Pointers are especially useful when a function needs to modify a variable that was created outside the function. 1. Basic idea Suppose we have: Cint x = 10; Here: x contains the value 10. &x means "the address of x." A pointer can store that address. Cint *p = &x; Now: x → 10 &p → address of x p → address of x *p → 10 The * operator is used to dereference the pointer, meaning "access the value stored at the address." 2. Modifying a variable through a function Consider this example: C#include <stdio.h> void increment(int *p) { *p = *p + 1; } int main() { int x = 10; printf("Before: %d
", x); increment(&x); printf("After: %d
", x); return 0; } Output: Before: 10 After: 11 What happens? When we call: Cincrement(&x); we pass the address of x, not its value. The function receives that address: Cvoid increment(int *p) So p points to x. Inside the function: C*p = *p + 1; means: Go to the memory location pointed to by p, get its value, add 1, and store the result back there. Therefore: Before: x = 10 p ──────► x Inside increment(): *p = 10 *p = 10 + 1 *p = 11 After: x = 11 3. Why not just pass x? Consider: Cvoid increment(int x) { x = x + 1; } and: Cint main() { int x = 10; increment(x); printf("%d", x); } The output is: 10 Why? C passes the value of x to the function. The function receives its own copy: main() increment() x = 10 ──copy──► x = 10 │ └── becomes 11 original x remains 10 With a pointer, the function receives the address of the original variable: main() increment() x = 10 ▲ │ └──────── p Therefore, changing *p changes the original x. 4. The three important pointer operations & — address-of C&x means: Give me the memory address of x. * — dereference C*p means: Give me the value stored at the address contained in p. int *p means: Declare p as a pointer to an int. So this: Cint x = 10; int *p = &x; can be read as: Create an integer x, then create a pointer p that points to x. 5. A more practical example: swapping two variables Pointers become especially useful when a function needs to modify multiple variables. C#include <stdio.h> void swap(int *a, int *b) { int temp = *a; *a = *b; *b = temp; } int main() { int x = 10; int y = 20; printf("Before: x = %d, y = %d
", x, y); swap(&x, &y); printf("After: x = %d, y = %d
", x, y); return 0; } Output: Before: x = 10, y = 20 After: x = 20, y = 10 The key idea is: Cswap(&x, &y); passes the addresses, allowing swap() to modify the original variables. Remember &variable → address of variable *pointer → value at that address So the general pattern for modifying a variable inside a C function is: Cvoid function(int *p) { *p = ...; // modify original variable } int x = ...; function(&x); // pass its address This mechanism is fundamental to C and is also heavily used with arrays, strings, dynamic memory, structures, and data structures such as linked lists.

prompt: Explain the difference between pass-by-value and pass-by-reference in C++ with code.
chatgpt_response: In C++, pass-by-value and pass-by-reference describe how arguments are given to a function. The main difference is: Pass-by-value: the function receives a copy of the variable. Pass-by-reference: the function receives a reference to the original variable, so it can modify it. 1. prompt: Explain how to structure a multi-file C++ project with header files and a simple Makefile.
