Recognizing Prefix Sum problems Look for phrases like: "sum from L to R" "sum of every subarray" "range sum queries" "sum between two positions" "how many elements before position i..." "frequency/count up to position i" Classic clue You see: Many queries: L R and each query asks: arr[L] + arr[L+1] + ... + arr[R] Build: prefix[i] = arr[0] + ... + arr[i] Then: sum(L,R) = prefix[R] - prefix[L-1] So a potentially O(n) query becomes O(1). Example arr = [3, 2, 5, 1, 4] Prefix sums: prefix = [3, 5, 10, 11, 15] Query: sum(1,3) is: prefix[3] - prefix[0] = 11 - 3 = 8 4. A more hidden prefix-sum pattern Prefix sums aren't limited to sums. Suppose the problem asks: How many 1s occur between L and R? Create: prefix[i] = number of 1s from 0 to i Then: count(L,R) = prefix[R] - prefix[L-1] The general pattern is: If a quantity can be accumulated from left to right, consider storing its prefix value. This can apply to: sums counts frequencies parity character occurrences weighted values 5. Recognizing prefix sum + hashing This pattern is especially important. Suppose the problem says: Find the number of subarrays whose sum equals K. At first, you might think: Try every subarray which is O(n²). Instead, define: prefix[i] = sum of elements up to i For a subarray (j+1 ... i): sum = prefix[i] - prefix[j] We want: prefix[i] - prefix[j] = K Therefore: prefix[j] = prefix[i] - K So while scanning, keep a hash map of previous prefix sums. Recognition clue Whenever you see: "number of subarrays with sum/property X" think: prefix sum + hashmap especially when negative numbers make sliding windows impossible. 6. Recognizing bitmask problems Bitmasks often appear when there are a small number of yes/no properties. Look for: subset choose/not choose selected/not selected switches on/off enabled/disabled set of features combinations of small items each element can appear at most once The biggest clue is: n ≤ 20 or another small n. Why? There are: 2^n possible subsets. For n = 20: 2^20 = 1,048,576 which is often manageable. 7. Bitmask example Suppose: items = [A, B, C, D] A subset can be represented by four bits. 0000 → {} 0001 → {A} 0010 → {B} 0101 → {A,C} 1111 → {A,B,C,D} Bit i tells whether item i is selected. To test whether item i is selected: C++if (mask & (1 << i)) To add item i: C++mask | (1 << i) To remove item i: C++mask & ~(1 << i) To toggle item i: C++mask ^ (1 << i) 8. Recognizing bitmask for sets Bitmasks are also useful when the problem involves a small universe of categories. Suppose a string contains lowercase letters and you only care whether each character appears. Represent the set using 26 bits: a → bit 0 b → bit 1 c → bit 2 ... z → bit 25 For character c: C++mask |= (1 << (c - 'a')); Then two strings can have their character sets compared very quickly. Key question Ask: "Is this really a set of a small number of yes/no states?" If yes, a bitmask may be hiding underneath. 9. Recognizing two pointers / sliding window Look for: contiguous subarray contiguous substring longest/shortest segment at most K distinct elements sum ≤ K maintain a valid window Typical structure: left →→→ right →→→ Instead of restarting for every subarray, maintain a moving window. Example Find the longest subarray with sum ≤ K. If the array contains only non-negative values, adding an element can only increase the sum. That monotonic behavior suggests: two pointers + sliding window 10. Recognizing a monotonic stack Look for: next greater element next smaller element previous greater/smaller nearest element satisfying a condition histogram rectangle temperatures until a warmer day elements blocked by a larger/smaller element Example: For each element, find the next greater element to its right. A brute-force approach looks right repeatedly. A monotonic stack lets us process the array in O(n). Strong clue If the problem repeatedly asks: "What is the nearest previous/next element satisfying X?" Think: monotonic stack 11. Recognizing binary search beyond sorted arrays Binary search isn't only: Find an element in a sorted array. A more powerful pattern is: Can I binary-search the answer? Suppose the problem asks: What is the minimum capacity required to ship all packages within D days? You may not have a sorted array of answers. But possible capacities form a monotonic condition: capacity too small → impossible capacity large enough → possible So: false false false false true true true You can binary-search the boundary. Recognition question Ask: "If I guess an answer X, can I efficiently determine whether X is possible?" If yes, consider binary search on the answer. 12. Recognizing dynamic programming DP often appears when: There are overlapping subproblems. The answer depends on smaller states. You can define a compact state. Look for phrases such as: minimum cost maximum profit number of ways can we reach... choose some items best possible... previous decisions affect future decisions Ask: "What information about the past is necessary to make the next decision?" That information becomes your DP state. Example: dp[i] = best answer using the first i elements or: dp[i][j] = answer using first i items with state j 13. Recognizing graph algorithms Convert the problem into a graph when you see: cities and roads computers and connections dependencies prerequisites transformations states and transitions reachable/unreachable minimum number of steps Then ask: Unweighted shortest path? BFS Weighted edges, no negative weights? Dijkstra Negative edges? Bellman-Ford All-pairs shortest paths? Floyd-Warshall Dependencies/order? Topological sort Connecting components cheaply? MST / Kruskal / Prim 14. Look for mathematical transformations Sometimes the key is to change the representation. Example: parity Suppose the problem asks whether a subarray has an even sum. You don't necessarily need the actual sum. You only care about: even / odd So prefix sums can be reduced to a single bit: prefixParity[i] Similarly: XOR problems → prefix XOR divisibility → modular prefix values character sets → bitmasks coordinate values → compressed indices Ask: What information does the problem actually care about? Discard everything else. 15. Use brute force as a discovery tool This is an underrated technique. If you're stuck, first write the obvious slow solution. For example: O(n²) Then inspect what the slow solution repeatedly calculates. Suppose you have: C++for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int sum = 0; for (int j = i; j < n; j++) { sum += arr[j]; if (sum == k) count++; } } Notice that sum is repeatedly extended. That suggests: prefix sum Or suppose you're repeatedly checking membership: C++if (x appears in previous elements) That suggests: hash set/map The brute-force solution can reveal the optimization. 16. A practical pattern-recognition checklist When you encounter an unfamiliar problem, go through this sequence: Step 1 — What is the input structure? Array? String? Tree? Graph? Grid? Intervals? Step 2 — What is the operation? Sum? Count? Minimum? Maximum? Reachability? Ordering? Number of ways? Step 3 — Is the data contiguous? If yes, consider: prefix sums sliding window two pointers monotonic structures Step 4 — Is n small? If: n ≤ 20 consider: bitmask subset enumeration backtracking meet-in-the-middle Step 5 — Is there a repeated lookup? Consider: hash map hash set frequency array Step 6 — Is there an ordering property? Consider: sorting binary search two pointers greedy Step 7 — Is there a "next/previous greater/smaller" relationship? Consider: monotonic stack Step 8 — Is there a choice with overlapping subproblems? Consider: dynamic programming Step 9 — Can the problem be modeled as states and transitions? Consider: BFS / DFS / shortest path / DP 17. Pattern cheat sheet Problem cluePattern to investigateMany range sumsPrefix sumCount subarrays with sum KPrefix sum + hash mapContiguous segment + constraintSliding windowPair with targetHashing / two pointersn ≤ 20, subsetsBitmaskSmall set of boolean propertiesBitmaskNext greater/smallerMonotonic stackLargest/smallest in every windowDequeSorted data + searchBinary searchMinimum possible maximumBinary search on answerNumber of ways / minimum costDPDependenciesTopological sortUnweighted shortest pathBFSWeighted shortest pathDijkstraNegative edge weightsBellman-FordAll-pairs shortest pathsFloyd-WarshallConnect everything cheaplyMSTMany repeated prefix-like queriesPrecomputation 18. The most important habit Don't memorize: "This exact wording means prefix sums." Instead, memorize structural clues. For example: "Many range queries" ↓ Repeated calculation over a prefix ↓ Can I precompute prefixes? ↓ PREFIX SUM Or: "Choose any subset" ↓ Each item = yes/no ↓ Only a small number of items ↓ 2^n states ↓ BITMASK Or: "Next greater element" ↓ Need nearest qualifying element ↓ Previous elements become irrelevant once dominated ↓ MONOTONIC STACK The general contest skill is: Recognize what information needs to be remembered, what information can be discarded, and what the constraints allow you to afford. Once you develop that habit, unfamiliar problems start looking like combinations of a relatively small number of underlying patterns.

prompt: Explain how to read a problem statement carefully and extract constraints, input format, and traps.
chatgpt_response: How to Read a Contest Problem Statement Carefully In programming contests, solving the problem often starts before writing any code. A good approach is to convert the statement into four things: Problem statement ↓ What is given? ↓ What is required? ↓ What are the constraints? ↓ What can go wrong? ↓ Algorithm + implementation 1. Read the problem once without coding First, understand the story and the goal. Ask: What exactly am I being asked to output? For example: Given an array, find the longest contiguous subarray whose sum is at most K. Immediately extract: Object: array Task: longest subarray Property: sum ≤ K Important word: contiguous That last word is critical. A subarray means contiguous: [2, 3, 4] but not: [2, 4] if 3 lies between them. 2. Identify the input Find the section usually called: Input Don't just copy the input into your program mentally. Determine its structure. For example: The first line contains T, the number of test cases. For each test case: The first line contains n and k. The second line contains n integers. Translate that into: T test cases ↓ read n, k ↓ read n numbers ↓ solve This prevents a common mistake: solving only the first test case. Example Suppose the statement says: Input: 3 5 10 1 2 3 4 5 4 7 2 4 1 3 3 5 1 1 1 Your mental structure should be: T = 3 Test case 1: n = 5, k = 10 array = [1,2,3,4,5] Test case 2: n = 4, k = 7 array = [2,4,1,3] Test case 3: n = 3, k = 5 array = [1,1,1] 3. Extract constraints immediately The Constraints section is often the biggest algorithm clue. Look for: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5 -10^9 ≤ a[i] ≤ 10^9 1 ≤ T ≤ 100 Write them down. For example: n ≤ 100,000 a[i] ≤ 1,000,000,000 T ≤ 100 Now ask: Can I use O(n²)? For: n = 100,000 usually no. Can I use O(n log n)? Usually reasonable. Do I need long long? If you're summing values as large as: n × a[i] then potentially: 10^5 × 10^9 = 10^14 So int is not enough. Use: C++long long 4. Convert constraints into a complexity budget A useful rough guide: ConstraintUsually considern ≤ 20O(2^n), backtracking, bitmaskn ≤ 100O(n³) may be possiblen ≤ 1,000O(n²) often possiblen ≤ 10^5O(n log n) / O(n)n ≤ 10^6Prefer O(n)n ≤ 10^7+Very careful about constants/I/O These are guidelines, not strict laws. The actual time limit, language, number of test cases, and operations matter too. 5. Pay attention to multiple test cases This is a frequent contest trap. Suppose: T ≤ 100 n ≤ 100,000 You shouldn't automatically think: O(n log n) You should think about the total input size. If the statement says: The sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 100,000. then: Σn ≤ 100,000 This is much easier to handle. But if it says: T ≤ 100 n ≤ 100,000 without a total-size restriction, the total could be as large as: 10,000,000 That changes your performance calculation. 6. Look for words that carry mathematical meaning Certain words are extremely important. "Distinct" Means duplicates are not allowed or should be treated specially. [1, 2, 2, 3] has only three distinct values. "At least" x ≥ K not: x > K "At most" x ≤ K "Exactly" x = K This can completely change the algorithm. "Contiguous" Usually means: subarray / substring Elements cannot be skipped. "Subsequence" Elements can be skipped, but their order is preserved. For: [1, 2, 3, 4] [1,3,4] is a subsequence but not a contiguous subarray. "Non-decreasing" Means: a[i] <= a[i+1] Equal values are allowed. "Increasing" Sometimes means strictly increasing: a[i] < a[i+1] Check the statement's exact definition if it matters. 7. Check indexing carefully Statements may use: 1-based indexing while C++ uses: 0-based indexing Suppose the statement asks: Find the sum from position L to R. If positions are 1-based: L = 1, R = 3 means: arr[0], arr[1], arr[2] Be careful when translating formulas. A useful habit is to write: Statement: positions 1...n Code: indices 0...n-1 8. Check whether values can be negative This is one of the most important hidden traps. Suppose you're asked to find a subarray with sum K. If all values are positive: 1, 3, 5, 2 a sliding-window approach may work for certain sum constraints. But if negative values are allowed: 4, -5, 3, 2 the sum can decrease when you extend the window. That can invalidate the sliding-window reasoning. You may instead need: prefix sums + hashing So always check: Can a[i] be negative? Can K be negative? Can zero occur? 9. Check whether duplicates are allowed Suppose the task says: Find two different elements whose sum is K. Does: [5] K = 10 count? No, because there aren't two elements. What about: [5, 5] K = 10 Yes, if using two different positions. The word different elements may mean different indices rather than different values. This distinction matters. 10. Check whether modifying the input is allowed Some algorithms, such as: Quickselect sorting in-place partitioning modify the array. If the problem later requires the original ordering, you may need to copy the data first. For example: C++vector<int> copy = arr; Don't assume the input must remain unchanged unless the problem requires it. 11. Watch for overflow This is a classic trap. Suppose: n = 100000 a[i] = 1000000000 The sum can be: 100000 × 1000000000 = 10^14 But an int typically stores only around: -2.1 × 10^9 to 2.1 × 10^9 So: C++int sum; is dangerous. Use: C++long long sum; And be careful with expressions: C++long long x = 1LL * a * b; The 1LL forces 64-bit arithmetic. 12. Read the output format literally Output requirements may contain traps. For example: For each test case, print the answer on a new line. Then: cout << answer << '\n'; If the statement says: Case #1: answer you need exactly that format. Contest judges generally don't care about your explanation or formatting beyond what is specified. 13. Study the examples as tests, not just demonstrations Examples often reveal details that are easy to miss. Suppose: Input: 1 5 1 1 1 1 1 Output: 4 This might tell you something about: duplicates adjacent elements whether empty answers are allowed whether positions or values matter Try to manually reproduce the example. If you cannot explain why the example gives its output, you probably haven't understood the problem completely. 14. Look for edge cases before coding Create a small mental test set. Empty input? Does the problem allow n = 0? One element? [5] All equal? [3,3,3,3] Already sorted? [1,2,3,4] Reverse sorted? [4,3,2,1] Negative values? [-5,-2,-8] Zero? [0,0,0] Maximum values? Test mentally for overflow. These cases expose many incorrect assumptions. 15. Look for hidden assumptions A statement might say: You are given a permutation of 1...n. That is much stronger than: You are given an array of integers. A permutation guarantees: Every value occurs exactly once. Values are from 1 to n. No duplicates. That can enable specialized algorithms. Similarly: The array is sorted. is a huge clue. The graph is a tree. means: Connected Acyclic Exactly n-1 edges Don't ignore these guarantees. 16. Watch for special structural guarantees Statements often hide algorithmic advantages in one sentence. Examples: The array contains only 0 and 1. → exploit binary structure. The graph is a tree. → DFS/BFS/tree DP. All edge weights are non-negative. → Dijkstra may be applicable. The values are between 1 and 100. → frequency array may beat hashing. n ≤ 20. → subset enumeration/bitmask becomes possible. The array is sorted. → binary search/two pointers may apply. 17. Separate "what" from "how" While reading, don't immediately decide: "I'll use a hash map." First write: What is required? For example: Find number of pairs with sum K. Then: Constraints: n ≤ 200,000 Then think: O(n²) is too slow. Need to avoid checking every pair. Then consider: hash map sorting + two pointers This prevents you from forcing the wrong algorithm onto the problem. 18. A useful problem-reading template Before coding, write something like: PROBLEM: What exactly must be found? INPUT: T = ? n = ? Array/graph/string = ? OUTPUT: What exactly should be printed? CONSTRAINTS: n ≤ ? values ≤ ? T ≤ ? Total n ≤ ? IMPORTANT GUARANTEES: Sorted? Distinct? Positive? Negative? Tree? Permutation? TRAPS: 0/1-based indexing? Duplicates? Overflow? Empty answer? Multiple test cases? Large input? Special output format? COMPLEXITY TARGET: Probably O(?) This takes less than a minute once you practice it. 19. Example of extracting a problem Suppose the statement says: You are given T test cases. Each test case contains an array of n integers and an integer K. Find the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly K. 1 ≤ T ≤ 100 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5 -10^9 ≤ a[i] ≤ 10^9 The sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 2 × 10^5. Extract: Task: Count contiguous subarrays with sum exactly K. Input: T For each case: n, K n integers Important: - contiguous - negative values allowed - large n - total n ≤ 200,000 Algorithm implication: O(n²) is too slow. Negative values make ordinary positive-only sliding-window reasoning invalid. Likely pattern: prefix sum + hash map Data type: long long Notice how the algorithm becomes much easier to identify after carefully reading the constraints and traps. 20. The final 30-second checklist Before submitting, ask: ☐ Did I handle every test case? ☐ Did I understand 0-based vs 1-based indexing? ☐ Did I respect "contiguous" vs "subsequence"? ☐ Are duplicates allowed? ☐ Can values be negative? ☐ Can values be zero? ☐ Can sums overflow int? ☐ Did I use the strongest input guarantees? ☐ Is my complexity safe for the maximum n? ☐ Did I handle n = 1 / smallest cases? ☐ Did I handle maximum cases? ☐ Does my output exactly match the required format? The core habit A strong contest programmer doesn't read a problem as a paragraph. They gradually transform it into: Statement ↓ Exact task ↓ Input structure ↓ Constraints ↓ Guarantees ↓ Edge cases / traps ↓ Complexity target ↓ Algorithm ↓ Code The constraints tell you what is possible; the wording tells you what is required; the traps tell you what can make an otherwise correct algorithm fail.

prompt: Solve a LeetCode-style problem on rotating an array in place and compare three approaches.
chatgpt_response: Rotate an Array In Place Problem Given an array nums and an integer k, rotate the array to the right by k positions. Example: Input: nums = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] k = 3 Output: [5,6,7,1,2,3,4] The important requirement is in place: use O(1) extra space. Approach 1: Rotate one position at a time Move the last element to the front repeatedly. For: [1,2,3,4,5] k = 2 First rotation: [5,1,2,3,4] Second: [4,5,1,2,3] C++ C++void rotate(vector<int>& nums, int k) { int n = nums.size(); k %= n; while (k--) { int last = nums[n - 1]; for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) { nums[i] = nums[i - 1]; } nums[0] = last; } } Complexity Time: O(nk) Space: O(1) This is simple, but inefficient when k is large. Approach 2: Use an extra array The element at index i moves to: (i + k) % n So create another array: C++void rotate(vector<int>& nums, int k) { int n = nums.size(); k %= n; vector<int> result(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { result[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]; } nums = result; } For: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] k = 3 the mappings include: index 0 → (0+3)%7 = 3 index 1 → 4 index 2 → 5 index 3 → 6 index 4 → 0 index 5 → 1 index 6 → 2 giving: [5,6,7,1,2,3,4] Complexity Time: O(n) Space: O(n) Much faster, but it violates a strict O(1) extra-space requirement. Approach 3: Reversal algorithm ⭐ This is the standard in-place O(n) solution. The key observation is: Original: [1 2 3 4 | 5 6 7] After right rotation by 3: [5 6 7 | 1 2 3 4] We can obtain this using three reversals. Step 1: Reverse the entire array [1 2 3 4 5 6 7] ↓ [7 6 5 4 3 2 1] Step 2: Reverse the first k elements [7 6 5 | 4 3 2 1] ↓ [5 6 7 | 4 3 2 1] Step 3: Reverse the remaining elements [5 6 7 | 4 3 2 1] ↓ [5 6 7 | 1 2 3 4] Final result: [5,6,7,1,2,3,4] C++ implementation C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> #include <algorithm> using namespace std; void rotate(vector<int>& nums, int k) { int n = nums.size(); if (n == 0) { return; } k %= n; // Step 1: Reverse the entire array reverse(nums.begin(), nums.end()); // Step 2: Reverse the first k elements reverse(nums.begin(), nums.begin() + k); // Step 3: Reverse the remaining elements reverse(nums.begin() + k, nums.end()); } int main() { vector<int> nums = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 }; int k = 3; rotate(nums, k); for (int x : nums) { cout << x << " "; } cout << endl; return 0; } Output: 5 6 7 1 2 3 4 Why do we use k %= n? Suppose: n = 7 k = 10 Rotating 7 positions returns the array to its original state. Therefore: 10 % 7 = 3 So rotating right by 10 is equivalent to rotating right by 3. This also prevents unnecessary work. Comparing the three approaches ApproachTimeExtra SpaceIn-place?Main ideaOne-position rotationO(nk)O(1)YesShift repeatedlyExtra arrayO(n)O(n)NoMap old index to new indexThree reversalsO(n)O(1)YesReverse whole + two parts Best choice under LeetCode's usual requirement If the problem requires: O(n) time O(1) extra space use the three-reversal method. Important edge cases k > n C++k %= n; k == 0 No rotation is necessary. n == 1 The array remains unchanged. Empty array Avoid: C++k %= nums.size(); when nums.size() is zero. Check first. The key pattern The most useful insight is recognizing that rotation can be expressed as reversing sections: [a b c | d e f] ↓ right rotate by 3 ↓ [d e f | a b c] Three reversals transform: [a b c d | e f g] ↓ [g f e d | c b a] ↓ [e f g | d c b a] ↓ [e f g | a b c d] So the solution achieves the otherwise conflicting goals of linear time and constant extra space.

prompt: Explain how modular arithmetic and fast exponentiation are used in contest problems with large outputs.
chatgpt_response: Modular Arithmetic and Fast Exponentiation Contest problems often ask for an answer like: 3^1000000000 or the number of combinations modulo: 1,000,000,007 The actual number may have millions or billions of digits, so we never calculate it directly. Instead, we use modular arithmetic and often fast exponentiation. 1. What does "modulo M" mean? The expression: a mod M means the remainder after dividing a by M. For example: 17 mod 5 = 2 because: 17 = 3 × 5 + 2 If a problem says: Print the answer modulo 1,000,000,007. it means: answer % 1000000007 2. Why do contests use modulo? Consider: 2^100 This is already a very large number. Now consider: 2^1,000,000,000 It is impossible to store directly in a normal integer type. But perhaps the problem only wants: 2^1,000,000,000 mod 1,000,000,007 We can calculate the remainder without ever constructing the enormous number. 3. The most important modular rules For modulus M: Addition (a + b) % M = ((a % M) + (b % M)) % M Subtraction (a - b) % M = ((a % M) - (b % M) + M) % M The + M prevents a negative result. Multiplication (a × b) % M = ((a % M) × (b % M)) % M This is extremely useful. 4. Example: multiplying huge values Suppose: a = 123456789 b = 987654321 M = 1000000007 Instead of calculating an enormous intermediate value unnecessarily, we can repeatedly reduce: C++long long result = (a % M) * (b % M) % M; For many common contest constraints, long long is sufficient for this multiplication when M is around 10^9. 5. prompt: Explain how to use bitmasking to enumerate subsets and solve a subset-sum style problem.
chatgpt_response: Bitmasking for Subsets Bitmasking is a useful technique when n is small, typically around n <= 20–25. The key idea is: Represent each subset using the bits of an integer. For example, with: nums = [10, 20, 30, 40] we have 4 elements, so a 4-bit number can represent whether each element is selected. 1. How a bitmask represents a subset Suppose: mask = 0101 Read each bit as: bit: 3 2 1 0 ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ mask: 0 1 0 1 So: bit 0 = 1 → select 10 bit 1 = 0 → don't select 20 bit 2 = 1 → select 30 bit 3 = 0 → don't select 40 Therefore: 0101 → {10, 30} Another example: 1111 → {10,20,30,40} 0011 → {10,20} 1000 → {40} 0000 → {} 2. How many subsets exist? For n elements, every element has two choices: include exclude Therefore: number of subsets = 2^n For: n = 4 there are: 2^4 = 16 subsets. We can simply enumerate masks: 0, 1, 2, ..., 15 because: 0 = 0000 1 = 0001 2 = 0010 ... 15 = 1111 3. Checking whether an element is selected Suppose we're examining element i. We can test its bit using: C++if (mask & (1 << i)) For example: mask = 0101 i = 2 Then: 1 << 2 = 0100 0101 & 0100 ---- 0100 The result is non-zero, so element 2 is selected. 4. Enumerating every subset Here's the basic pattern: C++for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (mask & (1 << i)) { // nums[i] is included } } } This gives: Number of masks = 2^n Work per mask = n Therefore: Time = O(n × 2^n) Space = O(1) 5. Subset-sum example Suppose: nums = [3, 5, 7, 10] target = 15 We want to determine whether some subset sums to 15. Possible subset: 5 + 10 = 15 So the answer is true. 6. Brute force using bitmasks C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> using namespace std; bool subsetSum(const vector<int>& nums, int target) { int n = nums.size(); for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (mask & (1 << i)) { sum += nums[i]; } } if (sum == target) { return true; } } return false; } int main() { vector<int> nums = {3, 5, 7, 10}; int target = 15; if (subsetSum(nums, target)) cout << "Subset exists\n"; else cout << "Subset does not exist\n"; return 0; } Output: Subset exists 7. Let's trace one mask For: nums = [3,5,7,10] consider: mask = 1010 Bits: index: 3 2 1 0 ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ mask: 1 0 1 0 Selected elements: index 1 → 5 index 3 → 10 So: sum = 5 + 10 = 15 We found the target. 8. Returning the actual subset Sometimes the problem asks: Find a subset whose sum equals the target. We can remember which mask worked. C++vector<int> findSubset( const vector<int>& nums, int target ) { int n = nums.size(); for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (mask & (1 << i)) { sum += nums[i]; } } if (sum == target) { vector<int> subset; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (mask & (1 << i)) { subset.push_back(nums[i]); } } return subset; } } return {}; } For: [3,5,7,10], target = 15 one possible output is: 5 10 9. A useful optimization: calculate subset sums incrementally The previous method does n operations for every subset: O(n × 2^n) Sometimes we can calculate the sum of a mask from a smaller mask. For example: mask = 1011 Take out its lowest set bit: 1011 ↓ 0010 Then: 1011 = 1001 + 0010 So: sum[1011] = sum[1001] + nums[1] This allows all subset sums to be computed in: O(2^n) time. 10. Using the lowest set bit A common trick is: C++int bit = mask & -mask; This isolates the lowest set bit. For example: mask = 101100 Then: mask & -mask ↓ 000100 We can determine which element that bit represents. 11. Efficient subset-sum enumeration C++bool subsetSum(const vector<int>& nums, int target) { int n = nums.size(); vector<int> sum(1 << n, 0); for (int mask = 1; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { int bit = mask & -mask; int index = __builtin_ctz(bit); int previousMask = mask ^ bit; sum[mask] = sum[previousMask] + nums[index]; if (sum[mask] == target) { return true; } } return target == 0; } Here: C++mask ^ bit removes the lowest set bit. For example: 1011 0100 ← lowest set bit ---- 1000 So: sum[1011] = sum[1000] + value represented by bit 2 Complexity Time: O(2^n) Space: O(2^n) This can be significantly better than O(n × 2^n) when n is small but the number of subsets is still substantial. 12. Enumerating only non-empty subsets If you don't want the empty subset: C++for (int mask = 1; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { ... } If the empty subset is allowed: C++for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { ... } 13. A classic contest problem: partition into two groups Suppose: nums = [2, 4, 5, 9] We want to divide the numbers into two groups such that the difference between their sums is minimized. Total: 2 + 4 + 5 + 9 = 20 If a subset has sum S, the other group has: 20 - S The difference is: |S - (20-S)| = |2S - 20| So we can enumerate every subset and minimize: C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> #include <climits> #include <cstdlib> using namespace std; int minimumDifference(const vector<int>& nums) { int n = nums.size(); int total = 0; for (int x : nums) total += x; int answer = INT_MAX; for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (mask & (1 << i)) { sum += nums[i]; } } int other = total - sum; answer = min(answer, abs(sum - other)); } return answer; } int main() { vector<int> nums = {2, 4, 5, 9}; cout << minimumDifference(nums) << endl; return 0; } Output: 2 One partition is: [9] → 9 [2,4,5] → 11 difference = 2 14. Bitmasking vs normal subset DP This distinction is important. Bitmask enumeration Good when: n is small because: 2^n is manageable. For example: n = 20 2^20 ≈ 1 million That's often practical. But: n = 50 2^50 is far too large for direct enumeration. Traditional subset-sum DP If the target is relatively small, we can use: dp[sum] = whether this sum is achievable Complexity: O(n × target) This can be much better when: n is large target is moderate For example: n = 100 target = 10,000 Bitmasking would require: 2^100 which is impossible, while target-based DP takes roughly: 100 × 10,000 operations. 15. The important decision When you see a subset problem, ask: Is n small? If: n <= ~20 consider: bitmask enumeration If: target is small/moderate consider: subset-sum DP If: n ≈ 40 and direct 2^n is too large, a common technique is: Meet-in-the-middle which reduces the work roughly toward: O(2^(n/2)) 16. Common bit operations These are worth memorizing: OperationMeaningmask & (1 << i)Check whether bit i is setmask | (1 << i)Set bit imask & ~(1 << i)Clear bit imask ^ (1 << i)Toggle bit imask & -maskGet lowest set bitmask & (mask - 1)Remove lowest set bit1 << n2^n For example: C++if (mask & (1 << i)) { // element i is selected } is the most important one for subset enumeration. 17. The bigger pattern Bitmasking turns a combinatorial choice: element 0 → yes/no element 1 → yes/no element 2 → yes/no ... into a binary number: 101001... Then: 0 → empty subset 1 → one subset 2 → another subset ... 2^n - 1 → all elements So the mental model is: Small n ↓ 2^n possible subsets ↓ Represent each subset with a bitmask ↓ Check each bit to determine selected elements ↓ Evaluate the subset Most important rule If n is small and the problem asks you to consider arbitrary subsets, immediately consider bitmasking. For a basic subset-sum problem, the direct solution is usually: for every mask calculate the selected elements' sum check whether sum == target with complexity O(n·2^n), or O(2^n) if subset sums are generated incrementally.

prompt: Solve a problem about finding the shortest path in a grid with obstacles using BFS and explain state representation.
chatgpt_response: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Using BFS This is a classic application of Breadth-First Search (BFS). The main idea is: Treat every reachable grid cell as a graph node. Since moving from one cell to an adjacent cell costs 1 step, BFS finds the shortest path. 1. Problem Given a grid: 0 = open cell 1 = obstacle Start = (0, 0) Destination = (rows-1, cols-1) You can move: up down left right Find the minimum number of moves from start to destination. Example: 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 1 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 Start: (0,0) Destination: (3,3) One shortest path is: (0,0) ↓ (1,0) ↓ (1,1) ↓ (2,1) ↓ (2,2) ↓ (2,3) ↓ (3,3) That's 6 moves. 2. Why BFS? Think of the grid as a graph. Each open cell is a vertex. For example: (0,0) ---- (0,1) | | (1,0) ---- (1,1) An edge exists when two cells can be reached in one move. Every move has the same cost: cost = 1 BFS explores the graph level by level: distance 0 → start distance 1 → cells one move away distance 2 → cells two moves away distance 3 → ... Therefore, the first time BFS reaches the destination, it has found a shortest path. 3. State representation This is an important contest concept. Ask: What information completely describes where I am? For this problem, the state is simply: (row, column) For example: (2,3) means: row = 2 column = 3 We don't need to remember the entire path. Why? Because if we've reached (2,3) with distance 5, then the future possibilities depend only on: current position = (2,3) not on how we got there. So: State = (row, column) This is a powerful modeling principle: A good state contains exactly the information needed to determine future moves. 4. BFS state We can store both position and distance: (row, column, distance) For example: (2,3,5) means: We reached cell (2,3) in 5 moves. Alternatively, we can store only (row, column) in the queue and maintain a separate dist matrix. Both approaches work. 5. C++ solution C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> #include <queue> using namespace std; int shortestPath(vector<vector<int>>& grid) { int rows = grid.size(); int cols = grid[0].size(); // If start or destination is blocked if (grid[0][0] == 1 || grid[rows - 1][cols - 1] == 1) { return -1; } // Distance matrix vector<vector<int>> dist( rows, vector<int>(cols, -1) ); queue<pair<int, int>> q; // Start state q.push({0, 0}); dist[0][0] = 0; int dr[] = {-1, 1, 0, 0}; int dc[] = {0, 0, -1, 1}; while (!q.empty()) { auto [r, c] = q.front(); q.pop(); // Destination reached if (r == rows - 1 && c == cols - 1) { return dist[r][c]; } // Try four directions for (int d = 0; d < 4; d++) { int nr = r + dr[d]; int nc = c + dc[d]; // Check boundaries if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) { continue; } // Check obstacle if (grid[nr][nc] == 1) { continue; } // Check whether already visited if (dist[nr][nc] != -1) { continue; } dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1; q.push({nr, nc}); } } // Destination is unreachable return -1; } int main() { vector<vector<int>> grid = { {0, 0, 1, 0}, {0, 0, 1, 0}, {1, 0, 0, 0}, {0, 1, 0, 0} }; cout << shortestPath(grid) << endl; return 0; } Output: 6 6. How BFS explores the grid Starting at: (0,0) Distance: dist(0,0) = 0 Its reachable neighbors: (0,1), (1,0) have distance 1. Then BFS processes those cells and discovers: (1,1) and so on. Conceptually: distance 0: (0,0) distance 1: (0,1), (1,0) distance 2: (1,1) distance 3: (2,1) distance 4: (2,2) distance 5: (2,3) distance 6: (3,3) The exact queue ordering can vary, but the distance assigned to each cell is shortest. 7. Why do we need visited? Suppose we didn't track visited cells. We could have: A → B → A → B → A → ... A grid naturally contains cycles. For example: A -- B | | C -- D You could move: A → B → D → C → A forever. The dist matrix prevents this: C++if (dist[nr][nc] != -1) continue; Once a cell has been reached, we don't need to enqueue it again. 8. Why is the first visit shortest? This is the key BFS property. Suppose we first reach: (2,3) at distance 5. Could another path reach it in 3? No. BFS completely processes distance 0 before distance 1, distance 1 before distance 2, and so on. Therefore, when (2,3) is first discovered, no shorter path could still be waiting to be processed. This property relies on every move having equal cost. 9. State representation becomes more interesting The simple state: (row, col) works only when your future choices depend solely on your current position. But suppose the problem says: You are allowed to break one obstacle. Now (row, col) is no longer enough. Why? Consider reaching the same cell: (2,3) in two different ways: State A: (2,3, obstacleBreakUsed = 0) State B: (2,3, obstacleBreakUsed = 1) These states have different future possibilities. Therefore we need: State = (row, column, usedBreak) where: usedBreak = 0 or 1 This is one of the most important ideas in BFS problems: If two visits to the same location have different future possibilities, they must be represented as different states. 10. BFS with one obstacle break Suppose: 0 = open 1 = obstacle and you can break at most one obstacle. The state becomes: (row, col, breaksUsed) We can maintain: C++vector<vector<vector<int>>> dist( rows, vector<vector<int>>( cols, vector<int>(2, -1) ) ); Then the BFS queue stores: C++queue<tuple<int, int, int>> q; Each state is: (row, column, breaksUsed) The transition rules are: Moving to 0: breaksUsed stays the same Moving to 1: allowed only if breaksUsed == 0 new breaksUsed = 1 Example: C++struct State { int r; int c; int usedBreak; }; int shortestPathWithBreak(vector<vector<int>>& grid) { int rows = grid.size(); int cols = grid[0].size(); vector<vector<vector<int>>> dist( rows, vector<vector<int>>( cols, vector<int>(2, -1) ) ); queue<State> q; q.push({0, 0, 0}); dist[0][0][0] = 0; int dr[] = {-1, 1, 0, 0}; int dc[] = {0, 0, -1, 1}; while (!q.empty()) { State cur = q.front(); q.pop(); int r = cur.r; int c = cur.c; int used = cur.usedBreak; if (r == rows - 1 && c == cols - 1) { return dist[r][c][used]; } for (int d = 0; d < 4; d++) { int nr = r + dr[d]; int nc = c + dc[d]; if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) { continue; } int newUsed = used; if (grid[nr][nc] == 1) { if (used == 1) continue; newUsed = 1; } if (dist[nr][nc][newUsed] != -1) continue; dist[nr][nc][newUsed] = dist[r][c][used] + 1; q.push({nr, nc, newUsed}); } } return -1; } Now the number of states is: rows × cols × 2 so the complexity remains: O(rows × cols) up to the constant factor from the two possible usedBreak values. 11. General state-design pattern When solving a grid BFS problem, ask: 1. Where am I? Usually: (row, col) 2. What additional information affects my future? Maybe: keys collected walls broken energy remaining direction number of moves parity switches used Then include that information in the state. For example: ProblemStateBasic shortest path(r,c)Break one wall(r,c,breakUsed)Collect keys(r,c,keyMask)Limited energy(r,c,energy)Direction affects movement(r,c,direction)Break walls + keys(r,c,breakUsed,keyMask) This is often more important than the BFS code itself. 12. Complexity For a basic R × C grid: Each cell is processed at most once. Each cell has at most four neighbors. Therefore: Time: O(R × C) Space: O(R × C) For a state-expanded problem: R × C × S where S is the number of possible extra states. For example, with one wall break: S = 2 so: Time: O(R × C × 2) Space: O(R × C × 2) 13. When should you use BFS? A strong clue is: Shortest path + every move has the same cost. Think: Grid ↓ Graph ↓ Each move costs 1 ↓ BFS If movement costs differ: 0/1 weights → 0-1 BFS non-negative weights → Dijkstra negative weights → Bellman-Ford Key takeaway The most important part isn't memorizing the BFS template. It's designing the state. For the basic problem: State = (row, column) For a more complicated problem: State = (row, column, information that changes future choices) Then BFS explores those states level by level: start ↓ distance 1 ↓ distance 2 ↓ distance 3 ↓ ... Because every transition costs exactly one step, the first time BFS reaches the destination state, its distance is the shortest possible path.

prompt: Explain how to stress test a solution using a brute-force checker and random test generator.
chatgpt_response:
Stress Testing with a Brute-Force Checker Stress testing is one of the best ways to find bugs in competitive programming. The basic idea is: Random test ↓ Fast solution ──────┐ ├── Compare answers Brute-force solution┘ ↓ Mismatch? ↓ Print the test case The brute-force solution is the oracle for small inputs. It doesn't need to be fast; it needs to be obviously correct. 1. Why use brute force? Suppose you've written an optimized solution for: Find the maximum subarray sum. Your fast algorithm might use Kadane's algorithm. But maybe you accidentally wrote: C++current = max(current + x, 0); instead of handling all-negative arrays correctly. Normal examples may not expose the bug. A brute-force checker can test thousands of random small arrays and compare: Fast solution vs Brute-force solution If they disagree, you've found a counterexample. 2. The three components A stress tester usually has three parts. 1. Brute-force solution Simple and trustworthy. 2. Optimized solution The solution you're trying to verify. 3. Random test generator Produces many small random test cases. Structure: C++for (int test = 1; test <= 100000; test++) { auto input = generateRandomTest(); auto expected = bruteForce(input); auto actual = fastSolution(input); if (expected != actual) { cout << "WA found!
"; printTest(input); break; } } 3. Example: Maximum Subarray Sum Suppose the problem is: Find the maximum sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray. Example: [−2, 1, −3, 4, −1, 2, 1, −5, 4] Answer: 6 from: [4, −1, 2, 1] 4. Brute-force solution For every starting position, extend the subarray and calculate its sum. C++int bruteForce(const vector<int>& a) { int n = a.size(); int answer = INT_MIN; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int sum = 0; for (int j = i; j < n; j++) { sum += a[j]; answer = max(answer, sum); } } return answer; } Complexity: O(n²) That's perfectly fine for stress testing because we'll use small n. 5. Fast solution Kadane's algorithm: C++int fastSolution(const vector<int>& a) { int current = a[0]; int answer = a[0]; for (int i = 1; i < a.size(); i++) { current = max(a[i], current + a[i]); answer = max(answer, current); } return answer; } Complexity: O(n) 6. Random test generator We can generate: n = random number from 1 to 20 a[i] = random number from -10 to 10 For example: [3, -2, 5, -7, 4] C++: C++vector<int> generateTest(mt19937& rng) { uniform_int_distribution<int> nDist(1, 20); uniform_int_distribution<int> valueDist(-10, 10); int n = nDist(rng); vector<int> a(n); for (int& x : a) { x = valueDist(rng); } return a; } Using mt19937 is preferable to old rand() for random testing. 7. "; } // ---------------------- // Stress test // ---------------------- int main() { mt19937 rng(chrono::steady_clock::now() .time_since_epoch() .count()); for (int test = 1; test <= 100000; test++) { vector<int> a = generateTest(rng); int expected = bruteForce(a); int actual = fastSolution(a); if (expected != actual) { cout << "Mismatch found!
"; cout << "Test number: " << test << "
"; cout << "Expected: " << expected << "
"; cout << "Actual: " << actual << "
"; printTest(a); return 0; } } cout << "All tests passed!
"; return 0; } You would typically add: C++#include <chrono> for the seed. 8. What happens when a bug exists? Suppose the fast solution accidentally contains: C++current = max(0, current + a[i]); For an all-negative array: [-5, -2, -8] the brute-force answer is: -2 because the best non-empty subarray is: [-2] But the buggy solution might return: 0 The stress tester reports: Mismatch found! Expected: -2 Actual: 0 Array: -5 -2 -8 That's extremely useful because you've immediately obtained a counterexample. 9. Don't generate only uniform random tests Purely random tests aren't always enough. Suppose you're testing a sorting algorithm. Random arrays might mostly look like: [7, 2, 9, 1, 5] But bugs often hide in special cases. Your generator should deliberately include: Smallest cases [1] [] if empty input is allowed. All equal [5,5,5,5,5] Already sorted [1,2,3,4,5] Reverse sorted [5,4,3,2,1] Many duplicates [2,2,2,1,2,1,1] Negative values [-5,-1,-8,-2] Zeros [0,0,0,0] Extreme values Near the problem's limits. 10. Mix random and targeted tests A stronger generator might do: C++vector<int> generateTest(mt19937& rng) { uniform_int_distribution<int> typeDist(0, 4); int type = typeDist(rng); if (type == 0) { // Completely random } else if (type == 1) { // All equal } else if (type == 2) { // Sorted } else if (type == 3) { // Reverse sorted } else { // Small values / many duplicates } // ... } This is often much better than blindly generating random data. 11. Randomizing the size intelligently Don't always use the maximum size. Use a mixture: 70% → very small 20% → medium 10% → near maximum Why? Small tests are easier for the brute-force solution and are excellent for finding logical bugs. Large tests help expose: time complexity problems overflow memory issues For example: C++int n; int type = rng() % 10; if (type < 7) n = 1 + rng() % 20; else if (type < 9) n = 20 + rng() % 100; else n = 500; 12. Reproducibility is important This is one of the most important stress-testing practices. If you use: C++mt19937 rng(time(0)); and discover a failure, you want to be able to reproduce it. Instead, print the seed: C++unsigned seed = chrono::steady_clock::now() .time_since_epoch() .count(); cout << "Seed: " << seed << '
'; mt19937 rng(seed); If a failure occurs: Seed: 183746291 Mismatch found! ... you can rerun with: C++mt19937 rng(183746291); and reproduce the exact sequence of tests. 13. Even better: save the failing test When you find a mismatch: C++if (expected != actual) { printTest(a); // Stop immediately return 0; } Copy that input into a permanent regression test. After fixing the bug, test it again. This creates a growing collection of: known difficult cases 14. Stress testing different kinds of problems The same architecture works for many algorithms. Binary search Brute force: check every possible answer Fast: binary search Shortest path Brute force: enumerate paths / use Floyd-Warshall for tiny graphs Fast: BFS / Dijkstra Subset problems Brute force: enumerate all subsets Fast: DP / meet-in-the-middle Range queries Brute force: calculate each query directly Fast: prefix sums / segment tree / Fenwick tree String matching Brute force: check every starting position Fast: KMP / Z-algorithm / rolling hash 15. The oracle must be trustworthy This is critical. If both solutions contain the same logical mistake, comparison won't catch it. For example: Brute force ↓ same incorrect assumption ↓ Fast solution Both might produce the same wrong answer. Therefore the brute-force solution should be: simple direct independently reasoned preferably structurally different from the optimized solution For example: Fast: binary search + greedy Brute: try every possible arrangement is much safer than writing two slightly different versions of the same greedy algorithm. 16. Differential testing This technique is often called differential testing. You're comparing multiple implementations: ┌── Brute force Random input ───┼── Optimized solution └── Another implementation ↓ Compare outputs If: brute != fast you have evidence that at least one implementation is wrong. If the brute force is trusted, you've found a bug in the fast solution. 17. A powerful workflow When implementing a difficult algorithm, use this cycle: 1. Write brute force ↓ 2. Verify brute force manually ↓ 3. Write optimized solution ↓ 4. Generate small random tests ↓ 5. Compare answers ↓ 6. Find mismatch ↓ 7. Minimize the failing case ↓ 8. Fix algorithm ↓ 9. Add the case to regression tests ↓ 10. Stress test again 18. The most useful trick: minimize the counterexample Suppose the tester finds: [17, 4, 9, 2, 11, 8, 6, 3, 15] and the solutions disagree. That's useful, but you can often find an even smaller failing case. Try removing elements: [4, 9, 2, 11, 8, 6, 3, 15] Does it still fail? If yes, continue. Eventually you might discover: [4, 2, 3] This tiny case makes the bug much easier to understand. This process is called test-case reduction or shrinking. 19. Important distinction: correctness vs performance A brute-force checker is primarily for finding wrong answers. For performance testing, use large tests separately. For example: Small random tests ↓ Brute vs fast ↓ Correctness Then: Large adversarial tests ↓ Fast solution only ↓ Time + memory Because the brute-force solution may itself be too slow on large inputs. 20. Cheat sheet When stress testing, remember: Stress Testing | ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐ ↓ ↓ Brute-force oracle Optimized solution ↑ ↑ └──────── Random tests ─────────┘ | Compare | ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ Match Mismatch ↓ ↓ Continue Save testcase ↓ Debug + shrink Core principles Keep the brute force simple. Use small inputs for brute-force comparison. Generate targeted edge cases, not only random cases. Use a fixed/printed seed for reproducibility. Stop immediately on the first mismatch. Save every discovered counterexample. Use large tests separately for performance testing. The most important mindset is: Don't ask only "Does my algorithm work on my examples?" Ask "Can I make it disagree with a simpler, obviously correct solution?" That turns testing from manually guessing edge cases into an automated search for counterexamples.

prompt: Explain how to solve problems on parentheses generation and validation during coding rounds.
chatgpt_response: Parentheses Problems in Coding Rounds Parentheses problems usually fall into two categories: Validation — determine whether a string of brackets is valid. Generation — generate all valid combinations of n pairs. The key difference is: Validation checks an existing sequence. Generation builds a sequence while maintaining validity. 1. Valid Parentheses — Validation Problem Given a string containing: () {} [] determine whether the brackets are correctly matched and nested. Examples: "()[]{}" → true "([{}])" → true "(]" → false "([)]" → false "(((" → false The key idea: Stack When we see an opening bracket, we don't yet know which closing bracket will match it. So store opening brackets on a stack. When we see a closing bracket: It must match the most recently opened bracket. That's exactly LIFO, which is what a stack provides. Example: ([{}]) Process: ( → push ( [ → push [ { → push { } → matches { ] → matches [ ) → matches ( Stack becomes empty → valid. C++ solution C++#include <iostream> #include <stack> #include <string> using namespace std; bool isValid(string s) { stack<char> st; for (char ch : s) { // Opening brackets if (ch == '(' || ch == '[' || ch == '{') { st.push(ch); } // Closing brackets else { if (st.empty()) return false; char top = st.top(); st.pop(); if (ch == ')' && top != '(') return false; if (ch == ']' && top != '[') return false; if (ch == '}' && top != '{') return false; } } return st.empty(); } int main() { cout << isValid("([{}])") << endl; cout << isValid("([)]") << endl; return 0; } Output: 1 0 2. Why st.empty() matters Consider: ")" There is no opening bracket to match ). So: C++st.top() would be invalid. Always check: C++if (st.empty()) return false; before accessing the top. 3. Why must the stack be empty at the end? Consider: "(((" Every bracket is an opening bracket, so the stack contains: ( ( ( There are unmatched openings. Therefore: C++return st.empty(); is necessary. 4. Complexity For a string of length n: Time: O(n) Space: O(n) Each bracket is pushed and popped at most once. 5. Generating Valid Parentheses Now consider a different problem: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate every valid combination. For: n = 3 the answer is: ((())) (()()) (())() ()(()) ()()() There are 5 valid combinations. 6. Why not generate everything and validate? There are: 2n positions. Each position could be: ( or ) So there are: 2^(2n) = 4^n possible strings. Most are invalid. For n = 3: 2^6 = 64 possible strings, but only 5 are valid. For larger n, generating everything becomes wasteful. Instead, we should build only valid prefixes. That's where backtracking comes in. 7. The crucial invariant While constructing the string, maintain: open = number of '(' used close = number of ')' used There are two rules. Rule 1: We cannot use more than n opening brackets C++if (open < n) we can add: ( Rule 2: We can only add ) if there is an unmatched ( Therefore: C++if (close < open) we can add: ) This guarantees that the number of closing brackets never exceeds the number of opening brackets in any prefix. 8. Why close < open? Consider: "(()" We have: open = 2 close = 1 There is an unmatched (, so adding ) is safe: "(())" But consider: "())" At that point: open = 1 close = 2 We've already closed more parentheses than we've opened. The prefix is invalid, and no future characters can repair it. So we never generate that state. 9. Backtracking solution C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> #include <string> using namespace std; void generate( int n, int open, int close, string current, vector<string>& result ) { // Complete valid sequence if (current.length() == 2 * n) { result.push_back(current); return; } // Add opening bracket if (open < n) { generate( n, open + 1, close, current + '(', result ); } // Add closing bracket if (close < open) { generate( n, open, close + 1, current + ')', result ); } } vector<string> generateParenthesis(int n) { vector<string> result; generate(n, 0, 0, "", result); return result; } int main() { int n = 3; vector<string> result = generateParenthesis(n); for (string s : result) { cout << s << endl; } return 0; } Output: ((())) (()()) (())() ()(()) ()()() 10. Visualizing the recursion For n = 2: "" | "(" / \ "((" "()" | | "(()" "()(" | | "(())" "()()" The algorithm never creates: ")" "())" "(()))" because those prefixes already violate the rules. This is the important backtracking principle: Reject an invalid partial solution as early as possible. This is called pruning. 11. State representation For generation, the important state is: (open, close, current) But current is the actual partial answer being constructed. The counters tell us which choices are legal. You can think of each recursive call as: State = (open, close) with transitions: (open + 1, close) or: (open, close + 1) subject to the constraints. 12. A more efficient C++ implementation Repeatedly doing: C++current + '(' creates new strings. A common coding-round implementation uses one mutable string and backtracks by adding/removing the last character. C++void backtrack( int n, int open, int close, string& current, vector<string>& result ) { if (current.size() == 2 * n) { result.push_back(current); return; } if (open < n) { current.push_back('('); backtrack( n, open + 1, close, current, result ); current.pop_back(); } if (close < open) { current.push_back(')'); backtrack( n, open, close + 1, current, result ); current.pop_back(); } } The pattern is: choose ↓ recurse ↓ undo choice That's the standard backtracking template. 13. How many valid combinations are there? The number of valid sequences with n pairs is the Catalan number: C(n) = (1 / (n + 1)) * C(2n, n) For example: nNumber of combinations11223541454261327429 This grows quickly. Therefore, because the output itself is large, a generation solution cannot asymptotically avoid producing all answers. 14. Validation vs Generation ProblemMain techniqueKey conditionValidate bracketsStackClosing bracket must match stack topGenerate parenthesesBacktrackingclose <= open and open <= n Think: Validation: existing string ↓ check it ↓ stack versus: Generation: build string ↓ make only legal choices ↓ backtracking 15. Common coding-round variations The same ideas appear in many problems. A. Multiple bracket types "({[]})" Use a stack and matching pairs. B. Minimum additions to make parentheses valid Example: "())" Track unmatched opening/closing brackets. C. Longest valid parentheses Example: ")()())" Common approaches: stack dynamic programming two-pass counting D. Generate parentheses with constraints For example: Generate sequences with n pairs but never allow more than k consecutive (. Now that constraint becomes another piece of the state. 16. The key interview insight When you see a parentheses problem, immediately ask: If you're validating: Does the problem have nested matching? If yes: Stack If you're generating: Can I build the answer incrementally while rejecting invalid prefixes? If yes: Backtracking + pruning For standard parentheses generation, remember these two conditions: C++open < n means: I can still add (. And: C++close < open means: I currently have an unmatched (, so I can safely add ). Those two conditions are essentially the entire core of the solution.

prompt: Explain how to approach digit DP problems with a simple example counting numbers with a given digit sum.
chatgpt_response: Digit DP: Counting Numbers with a Given Digit Sum Digit DP is useful when a problem asks you to count numbers in a large range while satisfying a condition about their digits. A simple example is: How many numbers from 0 to N have digit sum exactly S? If N is small, we could enumerate every number. But if: N = 10^18 there are far too many numbers to check individually. Digit DP solves this by processing the number digit by digit. 1. The key idea Suppose: N = 527 We want to count numbers <= 527 whose digit sum is 5. Instead of generating: 0, 1, 2, ..., 527 we construct numbers one digit at a time. The important question is: What information about the digits chosen so far determines what choices are possible next? For this problem, we need: position current digit sum tight So our state is: dp(pos, sum, tight) 2. What does tight mean? This is the most important concept in basic digit DP. Suppose: N = 527 and we're choosing the first digit. We can choose: 0,1,2,3,4,5 If we choose 5, we're still equal to the prefix of N. If we choose something smaller, such as 3, then our number is already smaller than 527. Tight = 1 Our digits so far are exactly equal to N's prefix. Therefore, the next digit cannot exceed the corresponding digit of N. Tight = 0 We've already become smaller than N. Therefore, the next digit can be anything from: 0 to 9 3. Example Take: N = 527 Suppose we choose: 3 The number starts: 3__ Since: 3 < 5 we know: 3__ < 527 So the remaining digits can be anything. Therefore: tight = 0 But if we choose: 5 we still have: 5__ and must respect the upper bound 527. So: tight = 1 4. State definition We'll use: dp(pos, sum, tight) where: pos Which digit we're currently processing. For 527: pos = 0 → hundreds pos = 1 → tens pos = 2 → units sum Digit sum accumulated so far. tight Whether the digits selected so far are exactly equal to the prefix of N. 5. State transition Suppose the current digit of N is: limit = digits[pos] If: tight = 1 we can choose: digit = 0 ... limit If: tight = 0 we can choose: digit = 0 ... 9 So: C++int limit = tight ? digits[pos] : 9; For each possible digit: newSum = sum + digit And the new tight value is: newTight = tight && (digit == limitDigit) More precisely: C++newTight = tight && (digit == digits[pos]); 6. Base case When we've processed all digits: pos == number of digits we ask: Did we get the required digit sum? If: sum == target return 1. Otherwise: return 0 So: C++if (pos == digits.size()) { return sum == target; } 7. C++ implementation C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> #include <string> #include <cstring> using namespace std; class DigitDP { vector<int> digits; int target; long long memo[20][172][2]; bool visited[20][172][2]; long long solve( int pos, int sum, int tight ) { // Sum already too large if (sum > target) return 0; // All digits processed if (pos == digits.size()) { return sum == target; } if (visited[pos][sum][tight]) return memo[pos][sum][tight]; visited[pos][sum][tight] = true; int limit = tight ? digits[pos] : 9; long long answer = 0; for (int digit = 0; digit <= limit; digit++) { int newSum = sum + digit; int newTight = tight && (digit == digits[pos]); answer += solve( pos + 1, newSum, newTight ); } return memo[pos][sum][tight] = answer; } public: long long countNumbers( long long N, int targetSum ) { if (N < 0) return 0; string s = to_string(N); for (char c : s) digits.push_back(c - '0'); target = targetSum; memset(visited, false, sizeof(visited)); return solve(0, 0, 1); } }; int main() { DigitDP dp; cout << dp.countNumbers(527, 5) << endl; return 0; } The output is: 9 So there are 9 numbers from 0 to 527 whose digit sum is 5. They are: 5 14 23 32 41 50 104 113 122 Actually, note that the full list also includes numbers like 203, 212, 221, 230, 302, etc.; therefore the count above would be incorrect if the implementation/list mismatch occurs. Let's verify the actual count carefully: for 0..527 with digit sum 5, the valid numbers are: 5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50, 104, 113, 122, 131, 140, 203, 212, 221, 230, 302, 311, 320, 401, 410, 500 So the correct answer is 21. The DP code itself returns 21; the earlier 9 output was incorrect. 8. Why leading zeros work This is an extremely useful trick. Suppose we're counting numbers up to: 527 The number: 5 can be represented as: 005 Its digit sum is still: 0 + 0 + 5 = 5 So Digit DP can simply treat every number as having the same number of digits as N. For example: 5 → 005 23 → 023 104 → 104 Leading zeros don't change the digit sum. This means we don't need a separate state for "has the number started?" for this particular problem. 9. Why memoization is necessary Without memoization, many different prefixes can lead to the same state. For example: dp(pos=2, sum=5, tight=0) might be reached through many different prefixes. Once we calculate that state, the answer for it doesn't change. So store: memo[pos][sum][tight] Then: same state ↓ return saved answer This converts an enormous recursion tree into a small number of states. 10. How many states are there? For a 64-bit number, there are at most about 19–20 digits. The digit sum is at most: 9 × 20 = 180 The tight flag has only two values: 0 or 1 So the number of states is approximately: 20 × 181 × 2 which is tiny. Each state tries at most 10 digits. Therefore the complexity is roughly: O(number_of_digits × maximum_sum × 10) For a fixed target sum, this is essentially very small. 11. The general Digit DP template Most digit-DP problems can be understood through: dp(position, state, tight) Sometimes there's another flag: dp(position, state, tight, started) The standard structure is: C++long long solve(int pos, State state, bool tight) { if (pos == digits.size()) { return isValid(state); } if (memoized) return memo[pos][state][tight]; int limit = tight ? digits[pos] : 9; long long answer = 0; for (int digit = 0; digit <= limit; digit++) { State newState = update(state, digit); bool newTight = tight && (digit == digits[pos]); answer += solve( pos + 1, newState, newTight ); } return memo[pos][state][tight] = answer; } The difficult part isn't the recursion itself. The difficult part is identifying the correct state. 12. When do you need started? Consider a problem such as: Count numbers that contain the digit 7. Now leading zeros matter conceptually. For: 5 we represent it as: 005 But we shouldn't say that the leading zeros are actual digits of the number. Usually we add: started = 0/1 meaning: started = 0 → haven't placed a non-leading-zero digit started = 1 → number has started Then the state becomes: dp(pos, state, tight, started) This is useful for conditions involving: number of digits leading zeros digit occurrence distinct digits digit patterns 13. Example of a richer state Suppose the problem asks: Count numbers <= N containing exactly three 7s. We might use: dp(pos, count7, tight, started) where: count7 = number of 7s seen so far When choosing digit d: C++newCount7 = count7 + (d == 7); If: newCount7 > 3 we can prune that state. The important point is that we're not storing the entire prefix. We're storing only the information necessary for future decisions. 14. Digit DP on a range [L, R] A very common contest pattern is: Count numbers in [L, R] satisfying some digit condition. Don't usually build a DP specifically for both boundaries. Instead define: F(N) = number of valid numbers from 0 to N Then: answer = F(R) - F(L - 1) For example: count(L, R) = count(0, R) - count(0, L-1) This is one of the most useful Digit DP transformations. 15. Recognizing Digit DP Look for these clues: N is extremely large. You need to count numbers from 0 to N. The condition depends on digits. You can't iterate through every number. The range can be converted to F(R) - F(L-1). Examples include: Count numbers with digit sum = S Count numbers containing digit 7 Count numbers with no consecutive equal digits Count numbers with exactly K non-zero digits Count numbers divisible by M Count numbers with a particular digit pattern 16. The state-design checklist When facing a Digit DP problem, ask: 1. What position am I at? pos 2. What property of the prefix matters? For digit sum: sum For number of 7s: count7 For divisibility: remainder For previous digit: previousDigit For a digit pattern: automaton/pattern state 3. Am I still equal to the upper bound? tight 4. Do leading zeros matter? If yes: started Then your state might look like: (pos, sum, tight) or: (pos, remainder, previousDigit, tight, started) 17. The core mental model Digit DP is essentially: Huge range ↓ Process digits from left to right ↓ Remember only relevant information ↓ Respect the upper bound using "tight" ↓ Memoize repeated states For the simple digit-sum problem: State: (pos, sum, tight) Transition: choose digit 0...limit Base: pos == number of digits Accept: sum == target And for a range: count([L,R]) = F(R) - F(L-1) The most important skill is state design: don't store the whole number prefix; store only the information that can affect the answer from that point onward.

prompt: Solve a problem asking for the minimum number of platforms required using sorting and two pointers.
chatgpt_response: Minimum Number of Platforms — Sorting + Two Pointers Problem Given arrival and departure times of trains at a railway station, find the minimum number of platforms required so that no train has to wait. Example: Arrival: [900, 940, 950, 1100, 1500, 1800] Departure: [910, 1200, 1120, 1130, 1900, 2000] We need to find the maximum number of trains present at the station simultaneously. For this example, the answer is: 3 platforms 1. Key observation A platform is needed when a train arrives. A platform becomes available when a train departs. So instead of comparing every pair of trains, separate and sort: arrivals departures Then process them chronologically. 2. Two-pointer idea Sort both arrays: Arrivals: 900 940 950 1100 1500 1800 Departures: 910 1120 1130 1200 1900 2000 Use: i = next arrival j = next departure At every step: If arrival comes before departure arrival[i] <= departure[j] A new train arrives before an existing platform is freed. Therefore: platforms++ i++ Otherwise arrival[i] > departure[j] A train has departed, so a platform becomes free. Therefore: platforms-- j++ Track the maximum value of platforms. 3. Why <= matters Suppose: Train A departs at 1000 Train B arrives at 1000 If the departing train leaves at exactly the same time the next train arrives, its platform can be reused. Therefore, under the common convention: departure <= arrival means the platform is free. So the implementation can use: C++if (arrivals[i] <= departures[j]) for a new arrival only when the arrival is not later than the earliest departure? Wait—the tie convention requires care. If arrival and departure are equal, departure should be processed first. Therefore the clean condition is: C++if (arrivals[i] < departures[j]) platforms++; else platforms--; This ensures an equal-time departure frees a platform before the arrival uses it. 4. C++ solution C++#include <iostream> #include <vector> #include <algorithm> using namespace std; int minPlatforms(vector<int>& arrivals, vector<int>& departures) { int n = arrivals.size(); sort(arrivals.begin(), arrivals.end()); sort(departures.begin(), departures.end()); int i = 0; // arrival pointer int j = 0; // departure pointer int platforms = 0; int answer = 0; while (i < n && j < n) { // A train arrives before the earliest departure if (arrivals[i] < departures[j]) { platforms++; answer = max(answer, platforms); i++; } else { // A train has departed, so free a platform platforms--; j++; } } return answer; } int main() { vector<int> arrivals = { 900, 940, 950, 1100, 1500, 1800 }; vector<int> departures = { 910, 1200, 1120, 1130, 1900, 2000 }; cout << minPlatforms(arrivals, departures) << endl; return 0; } Output: 3 5. Walk through the example After sorting: Arrivals: 900 940 950 1100 1500 1800 Departures: 910 1120 1130 1200 1900 2000 Process them: Arrival pointerDeparture pointerEventPlatforms900910Arrival1940910Departure09401120Arrival19501120Arrival211001120Arrival315001120Departure215001130Departure115001200Departure015001900Arrival118001900Arrival2 Maximum: 3 Therefore: minimum platforms = 3 6. Why this is a two-pointer problem The two arrays are sorted. We maintain: i → next arrival we haven't processed j → next departure we haven't processed At every step, compare: arrivals[i] vs departures[j] Whichever event occurs first gets processed. This is exactly the same general pattern used for: merging sorted arrays interval overlap problems meeting-room problems event scheduling counting simultaneous intervals 7. Alternative: Event sorting Another way is to combine all events: (900, arrival) (910, departure) (940, arrival) ... Sort them and process them chronologically. The two-pointer method is simpler here because arrivals and departures are already naturally separated into two lists. 8. Complexity Sorting arrivals: O(n log n) Sorting departures: O(n log n) Two-pointer scan: O(n) Therefore: Time: O(n log n) Space: O(1) extra apart from the sorting implementation's auxiliary space. 9. Common mistake: incorrect tie handling Consider: Arrival: 900, 1000 Departure: 1000, 1100 If a train departing at 1000 frees its platform before the train arriving at 1000, only one platform is needed. Therefore: C++if (arrivals[i] < departures[j]) is correct for that convention. If the problem instead says that a platform remains occupied through the departure time or requires a platform when arrival and departure are simultaneous, then the condition changes. Always follow the problem's exact definition. 10. The general pattern to remember For interval/resource problems: Sort start times Sort end times i = 0 j = 0 while events remain: if next event is a start: resource++ update maximum i++ else: resource-- j++ For this problem: arrival → platform needed departure → platform released So the answer is simply the maximum number of overlapping train intervals. The key insight is: You don't need to compare every train with every other train. Sort the two types of events and sweep through them with two pointers.

prompt: Explain how to solve string problems using the KMP algorithm and Z-function.
chatgpt_response: String Matching with KMP and the Z-Function Two classic linear-time string algorithms are: KMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt) — especially useful for finding a pattern inside a text. Z-function — computes how much each suffix of a string matches its prefix; it can also solve pattern matching. Both avoid repeatedly comparing characters that we already know about. 1. The basic string-matching problem Given: Text = "ababcabcabababd" Pattern = "ababd" find where the pattern occurs in the text. A naive solution tries the pattern at every position: text: ababcabcabababd pattern: ababd In the worst case, this can take: O(n × m) where: n = text length m = pattern length KMP and Z-function reduce this to: O(n + m) 2. KMP: the key idea KMP preprocesses the pattern. It builds an array usually called: LPS meaning: Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffix For every position i, lps[i] tells us how much of the pattern is still useful after a mismatch. 3. What is a proper prefix? Consider: "abab" Prefixes: "" "a" "ab" "aba" "abab" Suffixes: "" "b" "ab" "bab" "abab" The longest prefix that is also a suffix is: "ab" Its length is: 2 So: lps[3] = 2 4. Example of the LPS array Pattern: ababaca The LPS array is: index: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 char: a b a b a c a lps: 0 0 1 2 3 0 1 For example, at index 4: ababa The longest proper prefix that is also a suffix is: aba so: lps[4] = 3 5. Why LPS is useful Suppose we're matching: pattern = ababaca and we've matched: ababa but the next character fails. A naive algorithm might restart from the beginning. KMP knows: ababa has a prefix/suffix: aba So we don't need to throw away all our progress. We can continue from: aba This is the central KMP idea: After a mismatch, reuse the longest prefix that is already known to match. 6. Building the LPS array C++: C++vector<int> buildLPS(const string& pattern) { int m = pattern.size(); vector<int> lps(m, 0); int len = 0; int i = 1; while (i < m) { if (pattern[i] == pattern[len]) { len++; lps[i] = len; i++; } else { if (len != 0) { len = lps[len - 1]; } else { lps[i] = 0; i++; } } } return lps; } Notice the important line: C++len = lps[len - 1]; We don't reset len to zero immediately. We ask: Is there a shorter prefix that could still work? That's what makes LPS construction linear. 7. KMP pattern search Once LPS is available: C++vector<int> KMP(string text, string pattern) { vector<int> lps = buildLPS(pattern); vector<int> positions; int i = 0; // text int j = 0; // pattern while (i < text.size()) { if (text[i] == pattern[j]) { i++; j++; } if (j == pattern.size()) { positions.push_back(i - j); // Continue searching for overlapping matches j = lps[j - 1]; } else if (i < text.size() && text[i] != pattern[j]) { if (j != 0) { j = lps[j - 1]; } else { i++; } } } return positions; } Example: C++string text = "abababab"; string pattern = "abab"; vector<int> positions = KMP(text, pattern); The pattern occurs at: 0 2 4 Notice that matches overlap. 8. KMP complexity Building LPS: O(m) Searching: O(n) Total: O(n + m) Space: O(m) 9. Z-function The Z-function takes a different approach. For a string: s define: Z[i] as: The length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of s. Usually: Z[0] = 0 by convention. 10. Simple example Consider: s = "aabxaab" The prefix is: "aabxaab" At index 4, the substring is: "aab" which matches the prefix: "aab" So: Z[4] = 3 The Z-array is: index: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 char: a a b x a a b Z: 0 1 0 0 3 1 0 11. Z-function implementation C++vector<int> zFunction(const string& s) { int n = s.size(); vector<int> z(n, 0); int l = 0; int r = 0; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { if (i <= r) { z[i] = min(r - i + 1, z[i - l]); } while (i + z[i] < n && s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]) { z[i]++; } if (i + z[i] - 1 > r) { l = i; r = i + z[i] - 1; } } return z; } 13. Example: finding the longest border Suppose: s = "ababcab" Calculate the Z-array. If: i + Z[i] == n then the prefix of length Z[i] is also a suffix. So: border length = Z[i] for appropriate i. A useful mental comparison Think of KMP as: Pattern ↓ Build fallback information ↓ Don't restart unnecessarily While Z-function is: Whole string ↓ For each position: How much matches the prefix?
